17.title: The marketplace that learned to hold the wrench
17.fact: Thursday 22 October 2026, long read. Zetwerk Manufacturing Businesses lists on BSE and NSE tomorrow, Friday 23 October, at ₹151 a share. Four friends from IIT Madras incorporated it in December 2017 and started operating in May 2018 as a software company. It became something else entirely - twice.
17.intro: This piece is built from primary documents - the red herring prospectus above all - plus the Forbes India profile written at the unicorn moment, funding reports in Mint, entrackr and The Hindu BusinessLine, and PTI's final subscription tally. The appendix at the end boxes the figures with their sources and dates.

blocks.html: Towards the end of 2017, Amrit Acharya had a problem that looked nothing like a problem. He was an IIT Madras graduate with four years at ITC, a Berkeley MBA and a high-paying job at McKinsey in San Francisco. Two things wore him down. The advisory life meant, as he later put it, "you never knew what was going to happen to that advice". And his US visa situation had gone bad enough that his firm suggested a migratory arrangement - six months in Australia, then maybe six months somewhere new. When the second rotation came up, he snapped. His girlfriend, now his wife, settled it: "Uncertainty is not a bad thing necessarily." They flew home in January 2018.

His father was less lyrical. "I don't want to introduce you as my unemployed son to any of my relatives," he told Acharya, and gave him a deadline: figure out the next move before the wedding. So in May 2018, with three IIT friends - Srinath Ramakkrushnan, Vishal Chaudhary and Rahul Sharma - Acharya started Zetwerk. The plan was B2B software: tools to help companies manage their supply chains. Within a month they had a $1.5 million seed term sheet from Kae Capital and Sequoia.

Then, in June 2018 - before a rupee of that seed money had reached the bank - they pivoted. The software would become a marketplace instead: a place where companies could discover custom-manufacturing suppliers. Acharya had to call investors who had signed for a SaaS company and tell them it was now a different business. "We were worried. We did not know how they would react," he recalled to Forbes India. Both stayed. It was the first of two escapes that made the company.
Source: Forbes India, 30 Aug 2021

The marketplace ran into a human problem immediately. Zetwerk's suppliers were small and mid-sized factories - many in places like Chhattisgarh - and to them a new customer was not an opportunity; it was a risk. Would this unknown Bengaluru company pay on time? Were there hidden terms? "You Google us, and you would see nothing," Acharya said of the one-room-office days. The founders spent months convincing factory owners that the order on the screen was real money.

In December 2018, Accel's Prayank Swaroop was circling a $9 million investment and doing his calls. The B2B experts he phoned were nearly unanimous: Zetwerk would stay a small business - a "vitamin", nice to have. Then he called the customers. They described something else: a "painkiller" they could not ship without. "That was the moment of truth for me," Swaroop said. Accel's term sheet was ready in under ten days. The diligence lesson outlived the deal: experts price categories, customers price pain.

But the customers' pain turned out to be deeper than discovery. Suppliers found on the platform missed deadlines - for capacity reasons, financing reasons, logistics reasons. A pure marketplace could introduce buyer and factory; it could not make the factory deliver. So Zetwerk pivoted a second time, and this one was the real company: it became the supplier of record. A customer orders from Zetwerk; Zetwerk owes the delivery; behind the curtain, it splits the order across multiple small factories running in parallel - "parallel manufacturing", Swaroop called it. The marketplace had learned to hold the wrench.

They got plenty wrong along the way, and Acharya admits the biggest self-inflicted one: "We got very experienced senior folks too early in our journey." The perfectionist veterans and the break-things young engineers never fused. Half the company's early life also ran through Covid lockdowns - Zetwerk went remote-first, and Acharya has said he never met over half his own employees. None of it shows in the unicorn headlines; all of it is in the prospectus's risk factors, which still warn that its third-party suppliers can fail on capacity, quality and components.
Source: Forbes India, 30 Aug 2021 / Zetwerk RHP, Oct 2026 (risk factors)

groups.heading: Part three: the number that stopped growing

blocks.html: The growth was real. Revenue went from ₹21 crore in FY19 to ₹949 crore in FY21. In August 2021, D1 Capital Partners led a $150 million Series E at a $1.33 billion valuation - by Forbes India's count the country's 26th unicorn of that year, in three years flat. Acharya insisted the tag he valued was different: Zetwerk was a profitable unicorn, which meant "the velocity of growth" would be sustainable and fundraising would stay "a choice in my hands".

Then the story left the script. The RHP filed this October shows revenue from operations of ₹12,364 crore in FY24 - and ₹11,332 crore in FY25. A decline, in the middle of the blitzscale years, in the year the IPO was being prepared. FY26 recovered to ₹15,913 crore. The bottom line needs care, because the filing carries it on three tracks. Losses from continuing operations ran ₹852 crore in FY24, narrowed to ₹215 crore in FY25 and widened again to ₹964 crore in FY26; adding the civil-infrastructure business the company chose to discontinue takes total restated losses to ₹918 crore, ₹371 crore and ₹1,606 crore across the three years. Underneath both tracks the operating trend is genuinely better: the continuing-operations loss before exceptional items and tax fell from ₹427 crore in FY24 to ₹81 crore in FY26, and adjusted EBITDA reached ₹421 crore in FY26. The headline losses are swollen by one-offs - FY26's ₹836 crore of exceptional items were primarily a non-cash charge for adjusting the conversion ratios on its share classes. The latest June quarter shows the same pattern: the continuing-operations loss was ₹64 crore against ₹881 crore a year earlier, while the total loss including the discontinued civil-infrastructure business was ₹733 crore against ₹1,368 crore - ₹669 crore of this year's from the business being wound down. The continuing track's narrowing says less about suddenly found religion than about the one-offs falling away.

The market had already said so once, privately. A $210 million Series F in December 2021, led by Greenoaks Capital, marked the company at $2.7 billion (Mint). Two years later, in October 2023, Zetwerk raised $120 million more at a flat valuation, Avenir Growth leading at ₹407.4 a share (entrackr) - flat, with the FY25 revenue decline still ahead of it. Close to $90 million raised across 2024 in installments, led by Khosla Ventures, nudged the mark to $3.1 billion (The Hindu BusinessLine). The IPO's ₹151 cap values the company at about ₹25,583 crore, roughly $2.7 billion (Mint) - level with the December 2021 dollar mark. The cleaner comparator is the share price in rupees: the April and July 2026 private placements closed at ₹171 per equity share on the RHP’s own conversion-adjusted basis, so the ₹151 offer cap prices about 12% below those placements. Note also that ₹407.4 and ₹151 are not clean comparisons: the exceptional charges above were primarily the adjustment of conversion ratios between share classes. The founders' answer to the stall was to grow into the question: FY26 revenue rebounded 40%, and the IPO followed.
Source: Zetwerk RHP, Oct 2026 / Mint, 29 Dec 2021 (Series F) / entrackr, Oct 2023 (Series F2) / The Hindu BusinessLine, Dec 2024 / Mint on the ₹25,583 crore valuation / Forbes India, 30 Aug 2021

Revenue from operations, ₹ crore. Sources: Forbes India; Zetwerk RHP, Oct 2026.

blocks.html: Which brings us to Friday morning. The issue - ₹2,830 crore of fresh shares for the company and an offer for sale of 144.5 million shares by existing holders, about ₹2,182 crore at the ₹151 cap - closed Monday subscribed 3.06 times - institutions at 4.73 times and non-institutional buyers at 1.40, while retail stopped at 73 per cent, the same caution Jio's retail book showed on day one (PTI). The anchor book had already committed ₹2,251 crore at ₹151: BlackRock, Goldman Sachs, Nomura, Capital Group, Norway's Government Pension Fund Global and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority among 99 funds (PTI). Respectable and unspectacular, next to the 136 times that defence-imaging firm Tonbo drew the same week. Zetwerk's unofficial grey-market premium faded from ₹14 on 15 October to ₹3.50 by 19 October, with none recorded at the last update. The document's seller table is the quietest drama in it. The two promoter-founders, Acharya and Ramakkrushnan, sell 14.23 million shares each - about ₹215 crore each at the cap - against an acquisition cost the RHP records as "negligible". Kae Capital, the seed investor who heard about the first pivot by phone, sells shares that cost ₹3.94 for a 38-times return. Peak XV's Investments V fund paid ₹6.31 a share. And one promoter-group entity, Creovate Innovation - which both founders also direct - sells shares acquired at ₹178.58 apiece, above the cap price: an underwater exit printed in black and white. The other two founders from the May 2018 photograph, Vishal Chaudhary and Rahul Sharma, are in the table as well, selling up to 1.71 million shares each - about ₹26 crore apiece at the cap - and CFO Ankit Fatehpuria - elevated to fifth co-founder in 2022, per Moneycontrol - sells up to 2.29 million more, about ₹35 crore. All four founders, and the finance chief, sell something.

One illustrative transaction holds the whole argument. A customer places a large fabrication order. A 2018-vintage Zetwerk would have emailed three factories and invoiced a fee. The Zetwerk that lists tomorrow signs as the supplier, splits the order across a dozen small plants, finances the working capital, owns the delay if a furnace in Raipur goes down - and books the full order value as revenue. That is why the top line is ₹15,913 crore and the margins are a contract manufacturer's, why even a year of 40% growth books a loss on the continuing track - ₹81 crore before one-offs, ₹964 crore after them - and why the listing is a question rather than a coronation: has the wrench-holding version of the company finally found the scale where the model's costs stop growing faster than its orders?

What would invalidate the bull case is visible in the same filing: if the managed model's execution costs keep eating the gross margin as revenue scales - if FY27 shows another FY25 - then Zetwerk is a low-margin contractor with a marketplace's valuation story, and the faded grey premium was the honest price all along. The cash line says the same: operations consumed ₹682 crore in FY26 and another ₹506 crore in the June quarter, and the fresh issue's stated uses are repaying borrowings and acquisitions the company has not yet identified (RHP). What would confirm it is simpler: a second straight year of growth with the June quarter's continuing-operations loss-narrowing intact. Tomorrow's open is only the first data point, and the least reliable one.
Source: Zetwerk RHP, Oct 2026 / PTI, 19 Oct (final subscription + anchor book) / chittorgarh issue page / investorgain live GMP table, 21 Oct 11:37 PM

Revenue from operations (RHP, filed Oct 2026): FY24 ₹12,364 crore; FY25 ₹11,332 crore; FY26 ₹15,913 crore; Q1 FY27 ₹4,118 crore vs ₹2,649 crore a year earlier. Restated loss, continuing operations (RHP): FY24 ₹852 crore; FY25 ₹215 crore; FY26 ₹964 crore; Q1 FY27 ₹64 crore vs ₹881 crore a year earlier - that year-ago quarter's ₹803 crore of exceptional items were primarily non-cash conversion-ratio charges. Total restated loss including discontinued operations (RHP): FY24 ₹918 crore; FY25 ₹371 crore; FY26 ₹1,606 crore; Q1 FY27 ₹733 crore vs ₹1,368 crore a year earlier, of which discontinued operations were ₹669 crore vs ₹488 crore. Loss before exceptional items and tax, continuing operations (RHP): FY24 ₹427 crore; FY26 ₹81 crore. Adjusted EBITDA (RHP): FY26 ₹421 crore, a 2.65% margin; Q1 FY27 ₹103 crore vs ₹31 crore a year earlier. Manufacturing order book (RHP): ₹13,062 crore as of 30 June 2026; ₹12,370 crore at FY26-end. Operating cash flow (RHP): FY26 minus ₹682 crore; Q1 FY27 minus ₹506 crore. Funding: seed $1.5 million (Kae, Sequoia, 2018 - Forbes India); $9 million (Accel, Dec 2018 - Forbes India); Series E $150 million at $1.33 billion (D1 Capital, Aug 2021 - Forbes India); Series F $210 million at $2.7 billion (Greenoaks, Dec 2021 - Mint); Series F2 $120 million, flat, ₹407.4 a share (Avenir Growth, Oct 2023 - entrackr); about $90 million across 2024 at $3.1 billion (The Hindu BusinessLine); April and July 2026 private placements at ₹171 per equity share, conversion-adjusted (RHP). The offer (RHP; chittorgarh; Mint): band ₹143-151, priced at ₹151, valuing the company at about ₹25,583 crore; fresh issue ₹2,830 crore; OFS 144,525,036 shares; anchor book ₹2,251 crore. Final subscription 3.06 times - QIB 4.73x, NII 1.40x, retail 73% (PTI, 19 Oct 2026). Grey-market premium ₹14 on 15 Oct, ₹3.50 on 19 Oct, none recorded at last update (investorgain, 21 Oct 2026, 11:37 PM; unofficial indicator). Listing: Friday 23 October 2026.

18.title: Seven years for the promise
18.intro: At five this evening, bidding closes on India's largest-ever public issue. The company being listed was promised to shareholders from an AGM stage in August 2019 - 'within the next five years.' It took seven. This is what happened in between.

blocks.html: On 12 August 2019, Mukesh Ambani stood before shareholders at Reliance Industries' 42nd annual general meeting in Mumbai and made two promises in one speech. The first was about debt: Reliance, which had invested nearly ₹3.5 lakh crore in Jio's digital infrastructure by then and carried net debt of ₹1,54,478 crore, would become a zero-net-debt company within eighteen months. The second was about the stock market: "We will induct leading global partners in Jio and Reliance Retail in the next few quarters, and move towards the listing of both these companies within the next five years" (full text of the speech, Business Today; firstpost's AGM report).

The arithmetic he was offering was seductive. Jio had upended Indian telecom in three years - free voice, data priced at a fraction of the incumbents', and a subscriber base that had blown past 300 million. The oil-and-petrochemicals cash cow that funded it was mature. If the old business paid down the debt and the new businesses listed, shareholders would own the future outright and unencumbered. Both halves of the plan had dates on them. Both dates would slip - one by a little, one by a lot.
Source: Full AGM speech text, Business Today, 12 Aug 2019 / firstpost AGM report / Mint on the zero-debt plan

What happened next, in the middle of a global lockdown, has no real parallel in Indian corporate history. Between late April and late June 2020, a procession of the world's largest investors bought into Jio Platforms - the holding company for the telecom and digital businesses. On 22 April, Facebook paid $5.7 billion (about ₹43,574 crore) for roughly 9.99% - the anchor transaction of the whole exercise, struck while the world's airports were shut, and the deal that set the price everyone else paid around: an implied valuation of about ₹4.36 lakh crore for Jio Platforms (computed from the disclosed stake and price). Silver Lake, Vista, KKR, General Atlantic, Mubadala, ADIA, TPG and others followed. On 19 June 2020, Reliance issued a press release whose headline did the counting itself: "Reliance raises over ₹168,818 crore in just 58 days" - ₹115,693.95 crore of it from Jio's new investors, the rest from a rights issue.

"I have fulfilled my promise to the shareholders by making Reliance net debt-free much before our original schedule of 31st March 2021." - Mukesh Ambani, Reliance press release, 19 June 2020. Net debt had stood at ₹1,61,035 crore on 31 March 2020.

On 15 July, at the 2020 AGM, Google closed the round: $4.5 billion (₹33,737 crore) for 7.7% and a board seat (Reuters). In all, roughly a third of Jio Platforms - about 33% - was sold for about ₹1.52 lakh crore (~$20 billion) in one pandemic year, and Ambani told shareholders the group was ending "our current cycle of capital raising" (Reuters, 16 July 2020). The listing half of the 2019 promise looked close behind: Bloomberg reported in May 2020 that bankers were preparing Jio for an overseas IPO within 12 to 24 months. Five years, it turned out, was going to be comfortable.
Source: RIL press release, 19 Jun 2020 (primary) / Reuters on the Google deal, 15 Jul 2020 / Bloomberg, 26 May 2020

blocks.title: Two deals that were not to be

blocks.html: The first crack appeared in the old business, not the new one. The August 2019 speech had also announced a non-binding deal to sell 20% of Reliance's oil-to-chemicals arm to Saudi Aramco for $15 billion - the final leg of the deleveraging plan. On 25 November 2021, after two years of valuation differences, the companies called it off (Reuters). Reliance said it would re-evaluate; the O2C stake sale never came back in that form.

The second crack was a phone. In late 2021, Jio and Google launched the JioPhone Next - a ₹6,500 smartphone meant to convert India's remaining 2G users into Jio customers, the hardware expression of the Google partnership. It flopped. Within six months the price had been cut about 40%; media reports put sales around two million units against ambitions near 50 million; inventory was liquidated, and Jio retreated to selling own-brand 5G phones instead (The Ken's reconstruction, April 2023). The lesson Jio drew was expensive and useful: distribution and price were never the bottleneck - the product was.

And the listing? The five-year mark - August 2024 - came and went with no prospectus. By the 2023 AGM, the Economic Times was running pieces explaining why the "RJio IPO dream shown by Ambani 5 years back won't come true soon". Reliance Retail, the other company named in the promise, remains unlisted to this day. The promise had not died; it had just quietly gone overdue, the way large promises do when nobody is forced to mention them.
Source: Reuters on the Aramco deal being called off, 25 Nov 2021 / The Ken on the JioPhone Next, Apr 2023 / Economic Times, Aug 2023

While the listing slipped, the business compounded. Jio's own annual report for FY 2025-26 - read for this story, not via summaries - records revenue from operations of ₹1,46,885 crore, up 14.6% on the year; EBITDA of ₹76,255 crore, up 18.8%, at a 51.9% margin; 524.4 million subscribers as of March 2026, each consuming an average of 42.3 GB of data and 988 voice minutes a month (Jio Platforms annual report, investor relations). Profit after tax for FY26 was ₹30,049 crore, per RHP figures cited in IPO notes.

The growth engine changed character over the seven years, and this is the part the 2019 audience could not have foreseen. Subscriber growth is no longer the story - India is connected. Pricing is. Industry-wide tariff hikes, led by Jio, have taken average revenue per user from ₹181.7 a month before the July 2024 hike to ₹206.2 after it and ₹215.6 in the June 2026 quarter (RHP figures as cited in IPO notes). The second engine is the home: fixed broadband connections grew from 11.2 million in March 2024 to 28.6 million by June 2026, and rental income from the set-top boxes and routers in those homes more than doubled to ₹3,907 crore in FY26 (RHP figures via IPO notes). Jio also built the country's only standalone 5G network - the architecture that does not lean on a 4G core.

Average revenue per user per month, ₹. Source: Jio Platforms RHP figures as cited in IPO notes, October 2026.

On 14 October 2026, Reliance announced that Jio Platforms had filed its red herring prospectus with SEBI (ril.com corporate announcements). The issue: 27 crore fresh shares at ₹1,065 to ₹1,119, raising ₹30,213 crore at the cap - the largest IPO India has seen, passing Hyundai Motor India's ₹27,858.75 crore (Fortune India). At the cap, the market is being asked to pay about ₹10.3 lakh crore - roughly $108 billion - which would make Jio Platforms India's fourth-most-valuable listed company on debut, behind only its own parent, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank (Times of India). It would also tip the RIL group's combined market value past the Tata group's.

Read the structure and you can see what the company wants the money to say. It is 100% fresh equity - not one of the 2020 investors is selling a share. Meta (through Jaadhu Holdings), Google, PIF, KKR, Vista, Silver Lake, Mubadala, General Atlantic, ADIA, TPG - all of them stay in at the IPO price. The proceeds have a deliberately unglamorous job: prepaying three external commercial borrowings - dollar and yen loans due March to June 2028, carrying 1.40% to 5.13% - about ₹27,500 crore of it in FY27, with general corporate purposes capped at a quarter of the raise (RHP figures via IPO note). This is not a cash-out; it is a balance-sheet swap, equity for debt, taken at a price the 2020 investors are happy to hold.

Which brings back the anchor transaction. Facebook's April 2020 cheque - ₹43,574 crore for 9.99% - implied a valuation of about ₹4.36 lakh crore (computed). The ₹10.3 lakh crore cap price is about 2.4 times that, in rupees, over six and a half years (computed) - a respectable, not spectacular, return for waiting, and exactly the kind of number a prospectus does not print. The sellers of 2020 became the holders of 2026: that, more than any grey-market premium, is the informed-money verdict on the price.
Source: ril.com corporate announcements (primary) / Fortune India on size and valuation / Times of India on the debut ranking / IPO note citing the RHP (labelled secondary)

Three things, honestly counted. The timeline: "within the next five years" became seven, and one of the two companies named in the promise - Reliance Retail - is still unlisted. The phone: the JioPhone Next was a misread of what would move 2G users, and it died in about a year. And the Aramco deal: the elegant 2019 plan to deleverage partly through the old business ended with the new business doing all the work. None of these is fatal; together they explain why this listing arrives in 2026 priced on pricing power rather than in 2021 priced on subscriber growth.

Which leaves today. Bidding closes at 5 PM, UPI mandates at 7 PM. The settled print after day two: 5.57 times subscribed on BSE data - institutions at 13.29 times their allocation, retail at 1.54 times, having crossed full coverage only on day two (BSE consolidated data as of 7 PM Thursday, via NDTV Profit's timestamped record). Allotment is expected Monday. The bell, if the schedule holds, is Wednesday 28 October.

Seven years ago the promise was made from a stage in Mumbai to a hall of shareholders who had lent the company ₹1.5 lakh crore of patience. This morning the grey market - unofficial, unregulated - prices the debut at about 22% above the cap. The 2020 investors, offered the exit, declined it. The question Wednesday answers is whether the public market pays ₹10.3 lakh crore for what seven years actually built: not the company that adds the most subscribers, but the one that decides what India pays to be connected.
Source: NDTV Profit IPO live blog (BSE data, 7 PM 22 Oct)
Figures in one place, with their sources and dates. Items marked "RHP via notes" come from IPO notes quoting the red herring prospectus; everything else is from the primary document named.

The business (FY 2025-26): revenue from operations ₹1,46,885 crore, +14.6%; EBITDA ₹76,255 crore, +18.8%, 51.9% margin; subscribers 524.4 million (March 2026); average use 42.3 GB data and 988 voice minutes per month (Jio Platforms annual report, jio.com investor relations). Profit after tax ₹30,049 crore; ARPU series ₹181.7, ₹206.2, ₹215.6; home broadband 11.2 million to 28.6 million connections; CPE rent ₹3,907 crore (RHP via IPO notes, October 2026).

The 2019-20 promises: net debt ₹1,54,478 crore and the five-year listing pledge (AGM, 12 Aug 2019, speech text); net debt ₹1,61,035 crore on 31 March 2020, net-debt-free declared 19 June 2020 after ₹168,818 crore raised in 58 days, ₹115,693.95 crore of it into Jio Platforms (RIL press release); about 33% of Jio sold for ~₹1.52 lakh crore across 2020 (Reuters, 16 Jul 2020); Facebook $5.7 billion for ~9.99% (22 Apr 2020); Google $4.5 billion for 7.7% (15 Jul 2020, Reuters).

The issue (October 2026): RHP filed 14 October (ril.com); 27 crore fresh shares at ₹1,065-1,119; ₹30,213 crore at the cap, India's largest (Fortune India); valuation about ₹10.3 lakh crore, fourth-most-valuable on debut (Times of India); proceeds to prepay ~₹27,500 crore of 2028 ECBs in FY27, general corporate capped at 25% (RHP via IPO note); anchor book about ₹8,110 crore placed 19 October; day-two subscription 5.57 times, QIB 13.29x, retail 1.54x (BSE consolidated data, 7 PM 22 Oct, via NDTV Profit); allotment expected 26 October, listing expected 28 October.

groups.heading: What would prove the thesis wrong

blocks.html: This story's working thesis is that the seven-year wait converted a telecom operator into India's consumer-infrastructure layer, and that ₹10.3 lakh crore is a fair price for the pricing power that comes with it. Three things would cut it down. First, the listing itself: a debut that breaks the ₹1,119 cap and stays below it is the market rejecting the price outright. Second, the ARPU engine: the FY24-26 revenue growth - about 15.8% a year, per RHP figures via notes - rests on tariff hikes, and hikes have a political ceiling; a stalled ARPU with 5G returns still building would squeeze the story from both sides. Third, the home: if broadband additions flatten before the set-top-box economics mature, the second engine arrives too late to matter. Watch the first on Wednesday, the second every quarter.

RIL 42nd AGM speech, full text (Business Today, 12 Aug 2019); firstpost AGM report; RIL press release, 19 June 2020; Reuters on the Google investment, 15 July 2020; Bloomberg on overseas IPO preparations, 26 May 2020; Reuters on the Aramco deal being called off, 25 Nov 2021; The Ken on the JioPhone Next, April 2023; Economic Times, Aug 2023; Jio Platforms annual report FY 2025-26 (jio.com investor relations); ril.com corporate announcements (RHP filing, 14 Oct 2026); IPO note citing the RHP; Fortune India; Times of India; NDTV Profit day-2 record

Quotes are as printed in the named sources. FY26 business figures were read in Jio's own annual report; figures marked "RHP via notes" come from IPO notes quoting the prospectus and are labelled as such in the text. The two valuation multiples (₹4.36 lakh crore implied in 2020; ~2.4x to the cap price) are computed from disclosed figures and labelled computed. The Ken is paywalled beyond its opening; the JioPhone Next figures are from its report as cited in the text.
Written 23 October 2026, on the day the issue closes, from sources published 2019 to 2026 as dated in the text.

19.title: The premium, not the shortage
19.intro: On Friday evening, Brent crude settled at $116.72 a barrel - up 6.2% in a week - while Saudi Aramco's headquarters stood empty and the actual oil kept flowing through the Strait of Hormuz at close to normal rates. Understanding that gap, between the price of oil and the flow of oil, is the only way to know what this week costs India. Worked out below, barrel by barrel.

blocks.html: The headquarters of the world's largest oil company told its staff not to come in. Saudi Aramco evacuated its Dhahran campus and moved employees to remote work after a series of attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement - the first such evacuation since the Iran war began in February (Reuters, reported by CNBC and The National). The attacks had turned lethal two days earlier: a drone aimed at the Shaybah oilfield in the Eastern Province killed two people and injured two, and a strike on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam killed at least two and injured eight, according to Saudi state media. Over 48 hours the Houthis also claimed the Defence Ministry in Riyadh, an Aramco site in Yanbu and Abha airport. The US State Department ordered non-essential personnel out of the kingdom.

The market's answer came in two prints. In the Gulf evening, Brent traded at $117.20. By the New York close, Brent futures had settled at $116.72, up 3.1% on the day and 6.2% on the week; US WTI settled at $103.27. And yet, inside the same day's reporting, sat the fact this whole essay hangs on. "Production and export flows through the Strait of Hormuz are still holding at close to pre-conflict levels, though at elevated shipping rates," said Edward Bell, head of research at MUFG, and Soojin Kim, research analyst at the group, to The National. The oil is flowing. The price is rising anyway. That difference has a name, a history and a cost - and India pays the bill.
Source: CNBC, 23 October (read in full) / The National, 23 October (read in full)

Eight months ago, on 28 February, Israel and the United States attacked Iran, killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other senior officials. Iran answered with strikes on Israel and across the Gulf, and asserted control over the Strait of Hormuz - the channel for about a fifth of the world's oil consumption (Reuters's Hormuz explainer; the US Energy Information Administration calls it the world's most important oil chokepoint). On 8 March, Iran named one of Khamenei's sons, Mojtaba, as the new supreme leader; he has not been seen in public since and is believed to have been hurt in the opening strikes. A two-week ceasefire followed on 7 April - Israel not included - and on 21 April, President Trump extended it indefinitely. It broke on 7 June, when Iran fired on Israel for the first time since April. A week later Trump announced an interim deal; it was signed around 26-27 June, starting a 60-day clock toward a permanent end to the war. By 12 July the deal was already fraying - strikes traded both ways, Trump threatening Iran's civilian infrastructure and musing about seizing Kharg Island, the terminal for most of Iran's crude exports. (All from AP's running timeline of the war, updated 12 July.)

October brought the next turn. On Monday, Brent had slipped from $110 as traders priced in more Russian supply - the war premium bleeding out, as it does. Then came Wednesday: Shaybah, Dammam, the claims on Riyadh and Yanbu, the Dhahran evacuation, the State Department pullout. Trump said Wednesday the US is "not negotiating" with Iran and something would happen "fairly soon"; US officials told the New York Times that plans exist for fresh strikes after the midterm elections. Iran's army chief told the Tasnim agency his forces are ready for "asymmetric warfare". Traders, CNBC reports, now expect US strikes to resume in the coming weeks. A Libyan supply disruption - real, but small - tightened the physical market just enough to give the fear somewhere to sit.
Source: AP war timeline (read in full) / CNBC, 23 October / The National, 23 October

groups.heading: The argument: you are paying for a strike that has not happened

blocks.html: A shortage is a physical fact: there is less oil than buyers want, and the price rises until someone goes without. A premium is a probability: there is exactly enough oil today, but a chance there will not be tomorrow, and every refiner pays a little extra to be sure of having it. Shortages are slow to form and slow to fix. Premiums form in an afternoon and vanish over a weekend.

This week is a premium. The flows through Hormuz are near pre-conflict levels (MUFG's read on Friday). Nobody's refinery has gone short. What changed is the perceived odds of a US strike on Iran and a Saudi-Houthi war sliding back into something wider - and crude repriced those odds by about $6.7 a barrel in five sessions. That is not a comforting fact, but it is a useful one, because premiums behave in ways shortages do not: they spike on headlines, they decay on quiet days, and they unwind completely if the feared event does not arrive. And the premium has come off before: by this Monday, with Russian supply prospects improving, the five-month rally was being openly questioned - Brent slipped back from $110 before Wednesday's attacks repriced it. The premium is real money while it lasts - it just does not last by itself.
The $116.72 print is not what oil costs. It is what the fear of a strike costs, added to what oil costs - and the two parts have very different shelf lives.

groups.heading: What it costs India, worked out once

blocks.html: India imports 88.6% of the crude it consumes (April to January of FY26, on Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell data via the Indian Express). That dependence gives the arithmetic its blunt edge: every $1 on the barrel price adds up to $2 billion a year to the import bill (the Indian Express's explainer on the PPAC data).

blocks.svg:
$1 per barrel$2bn up to $2bn a year (Indian Express on PPAC data)
This week's move, about $6.7$13.4bn illustrative, at the same ratio
For scale: the Jio IPO$3.2bn Rs 30,213 crore, about $3.2bn at Friday's rupee
Annualised import-bill sensitivity, US$ billions. Source: Indian Express explainers on PPAC data; the week's Brent move is $110 to $116.72.

blocks.html: Now the week's transaction, explicitly. Brent went from about $110 on Monday to $116.72 on Friday - call it $6.7. At the PPAC ratio, that is up to about $13.4 billion a year of extra import cost if it holds - an illustrative sensitivity, holding the import basket and the exchange rate constant, not a measure of what this week has already cost. At Friday's rupee (94.93 per dollar), it is roughly ₹1.27 lakh crore. The Jio Platforms IPO that closed the same day - the largest in Indian history - raised ₹30,213 crore. The week's oil move, on that same illustrative annualisation, is about four Jio IPOs. That is the size of the premium, stated in the week's own units.

The channels from that number to an Indian household are already visible. The rupee fell 12 paise to a provisional 94.93 on Friday, a second straight down day, with traders citing crude (PTI). HPCL's results on Thursday showed what the squeeze does to a refiner-marketer: profit down 9% year on year to ₹3,483 crore as higher crude prices and tax expenses squeezed marketing margins, even with product sales up 26% (Business Standard, Moneycontrol). BPCL's filing on Friday put the cumulative LPG under-recovery buffer at ₹17,334.40 crore - the shortfall the company has absorbed selling cooking gas below cost, with ₹3,796.98 crore of government compensation recognised in the half. At $116, the resolution runs through some mix of retail price changes, government compensation and refiner margins - the filing sizes the buffer; it does not say who pays.
Source: Indian Express on import dependence / Indian Express on the Hormuz-quarter import surge / PTI via The Hindu on the rupee / Business Standard on HPCL / BPCL NSE filing (primary)

groups.heading: The second bill: what oil does to interest rates

blocks.html: The first bill lands on the import ledger. The second lands on the cost of money, and it may be the larger one. Oil is the fastest-moving ingredient in inflation, and inflation is what central banks answer to. On Friday, CME's FedWatch tool - the market's own pricing - showed traders putting a 92% chance on the Federal Reserve holding rates at its 27-28 October meeting, but a 78% probability of a December rate HIKE (cited by CNBC). A hike: not a hold, not the cut that was the base case weeks ago. Last week's US consumer and producer inflation came in hot, and Friday's flash PMI showed selling prices at their highest since 2022 even as activity cooled (composite 57.6 against 58.4). The Personal Consumption Expenditures report on 29 October is the next hard number.

Watch what this did to gold, because it is the cleanest proof of the mechanism. Gold is the ancient war hedge - and it just had its worst week since June, down 4%, with spot trading at $3,998.49 on Friday afternoon (2:27 PM EDT) - under $4,000 for the first time since mid-July - while December futures settled at $4,007.90. Missiles flew and gold fell, because the missiles' effect on interest rates mattered more than the missiles: higher-for-longer yields make a zero-yield metal expensive to hold, and Thursday's AI selloff forced funds to sell whatever was sellable to meet margin calls (analyst Jim Wyckoff's account to CNBC). The same repricing reached Mumbai: midcaps fell 2.2% on a day the Sensex fell 0.2%, because long-duration assets discount at the new rate path first. India's 10-year government bond yield closed Friday at 7.47% - a tenth straight weekly rise, the longest losing streak for Indian government bonds in 30 years (Business Standard).
Source: CNBC on gold and the Fed (read in full)

groups.heading: What would prove this reading wrong

blocks.html: Three things would turn this premium into a shortage, and they are all watchable. First, a strike that hits Gulf production or loading infrastructure rather than symbols - the Shaybah drone killed people but did not stop a barrel; a hit that does stop barrels is a different market. Second, the Strait itself: Iran still insists it alone controls Hormuz, and thousands of mariners were waiting out the war's terms there as of July; any boarding, mining or insurance withdrawal is the physical threshold. Third, a strike-after-the-midterms scenario playing out in public, because it converts a headline risk into a dated calendar risk.

The invalidation runs the other way too. If the weekend passes quietly, if the interim-deal track revives - it survived one unravelling already - or if Russian and Saudi barrels visibly cover the gap (Monday's slip from $110 came on exactly that prospect), the premium unwinds as fast as it built, and the India math above shrinks with it. The honest position for a Saturday morning: the flows say calm, the evacuations say otherwise, and the price is the argument between them.

The week hands the decision to a single day. On Wednesday 28 October, in Washington, the Federal Reserve ends its meeting and tells the world whether the December hike is real; in Mumbai, that same morning, Jio Platforms lists at ₹10.3 lakh crore of valuation on the largest bid haul an Indian IPO has ever seen; and on Thursday the PCE report prints the inflation number both will live with. Oil will vote first - the weekend's headlines set Monday's open - but the premium's fate is decided by whether anything actually explodes between now and then. India, importing 88.6% of its oil, does not get a vote. It only gets the bill.
The one number to hold through it: $1 a barrel equals up to $2 billion a year. When the anchors shout $120 or $100 next week, you can convert it yourself, in the time it takes to read the ticker.

Sources read in full for this essay: CNBC and The National on Friday's oil market and the Gulf attacks; AP's timeline of the Iran war and its index levels; CNBC on gold and the Fed; Indian Express's oil-dependence and Hormuz explainers on PPAC data; The Hindu on the rupee; Business Standard on HPCL; BPCL's NSE filing; Indian Express on the Jio close. The import-bill arithmetic is shown wherever it is used.

20.title: The chairman's to-do list
20.fact: The long read, Sunday 25 October 2026. SEBI chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey has laid out an unusually specific market-plumbing agenda: tokenised corporate bonds, a short-selling review, graded broker compliance and rules for market AI. Two of the four are already past the starting line - the speech's real news is what the next phase looks like. This is the story of the list, what each item would actually change, and what would prove it is only a speech.
20.intro: One argument, worked through: the speech matters less for what it announced than for where it says each item actually stands. Two of its four big items are already moving - a bond pilot six weeks live, AI guidelines past consultation - and every item now has a next observable step.

blocks.html: ANMI's International Capital Market Convention - the broking industry's own gathering, at its sixteenth edition this year - is where SEBI's chairman, Tuhin Kanta Pandey, used the stage to read out what amounts to a work order for the market's next rebuild. Not a vision speech about grand themes: it runs four pillars - simpler rules, deeper markets, responsible technology, wider access - across about a dozen items. This article takes the four that would change the market's structure most.

The audience matters for reading the speech. Brokers are the industry that carries the compliance load, operates the lending desks and will run - or resist - every one of these changes. A chairman who tells this room that compliance will be graded by scale, client exposure and technology reliance, and that short-selling rules are under review, is not testing slogans. He is telling the people who will have to build it.
Here is what is on the list, what each item really does, and what has to happen next for any of it to be real.

groups.heading: Job one: bonds that ordinary people can actually trade

blocks.html: India's corporate-bond market is big and strangely invisible. About Rs 61 lakh crore is outstanding - the chairman's own figure - and almost none of it trades where a saver can see it. The market runs institution to institution, over the phone and through dealers, in ticket sizes built for institutions. A fixed deposit is simple but locks you in; equity is liquid but volatile; the bond in between, which should be the natural third asset, has let retail into eligible privately placed issues at Rs 10,000 since July 2024 - but barely lets it out, because secondary trading is thin and the exit is where the cost sits.

The chairman's answer has a name: Demat 2.0. In the 1990s, dematerialisation took share certificates out of paper and put them in electronic accounts, and equity trading exploded. Demat 2.0 is the same idea for bonds - and it is not a proposal. SEBI launched the pilot on 10 September: three issuers - REC, L&T and IIFL - have raised Rs 1,025 crore in tokenised corporate bonds, settled atomically against the RBI's wholesale CBDC and held in ordinary demat accounts. First-phase issuance was still running at the 10 September launch. The speech's news is what comes next: phase two, in which these bonds start trading in the secondary market; the launch release names the venue - the existing RFQ platforms - with retail access promised in a later phase.

To see what is actually being fixed, walk one transaction through both worlds. Today: you want to lend Rs 10 lakh to a solid company for three years. You can - since July 2024, privately placed bonds come in Rs 10,000 denominations and online bond platforms will sell you one. What you cannot easily do is sell it again: secondary trading is thin, quotes are wide, and the exit, not the entry, is the real wall between households and bonds. In the end state the chairman is pointing to: that company's bond exists as a token in your demat account, it trades on the RFQ platform, and settlement - the part that in the conventional market takes days - lands the same day, because the bond and the money move together on the RBI's CBDC rail.

Two dependencies decide whether this is real. First, market-makers - the speech separately lists a bond market-making framework, and it is the unglamorous half of the idea, because a token nobody quotes is a fixed deposit with extra steps. Second, the small print on credit risk: a retail-tradable bond market also makes it easier to sell weak paper to the least protected buyer. How the framework grades issuers will matter as much as the token itself.

groups.heading: Job two: let the market argue with itself

blocks.html: Betting against a stock in India is hard, expensive and rare. The mechanism for it - securities lending and borrowing, SLB, the pipe through which you borrow shares to sell them short - exists but stays thin, while futures and options carry most of the scepticism. The chairman said the short-selling framework and SLB are under review.

Why a regulator would want stronger shorts is not cynicism; it is price discovery. A market where doubt is expensive is a market where bad stories last longer. When sceptics cannot borrow stock cheaply, the first honest signal of trouble arrives late and all at once. A working SLB market lets the bear case get priced gradually instead of detonating.

Watch for the review's shape: borrow costs, eligible-stock lists, and whether large shareholders are nudged to lend idle stock. If the review ends in a consultation paper with real relaxations, crowded long trades get a new counterweight. If it ends in a study, nothing changes.

groups.heading: Job three: one rulebook, sized to fit

blocks.html: Ask a two-branch brokerage what compliance costs and you get a number that decides whether the firm survives; ask a bank-owned giant and you get a department. The chairman told the room - the room that pays these bills - that SEBI is exploring graded compliance: obligations scaled to an intermediary's scale, client exposure and reliance on technology - the chairman's three factors.

This is the item with the most immediate constituency and the least public glamour. Its second-order effect is competition: a compliance load that is flat in size is a moat for the big and a wall for the small. Grading it changes how many brokers can exist, which changes what distribution costs - and in a country where the same firms distribute mutual funds, bonds and insurance, that cost eventually reaches every saver's statement.

groups.heading: Job four: rules for the machines

blocks.html: The last item is further along than it looks. Market intermediaries already run AI - in surveillance, in client onboarding, in robo-advice, in order routing - and the regulator's rulebook is not a blank page: SEBI put out a consultation paper on the responsible use of AI and ML in June 2025. The chairman's news is that the final guidelines are now being finalised - tiered by risk, with clear accountability, data controls and kill switches, aligned with IOSCO, the global standard-setter's toolkit - plus a newer, earlier-stage idea: an AI sandbox the speech says SEBI is exploring, where new tools can be tested safely.

The detail to hold is "kill switches". A guideline that requires a market AI to be stoppable is a guideline written by someone who has read the failure modes: models do not get tired or conflicted; they get wrong, at scale, at machine speed. Tiering matters for the same reason - a chatbot answering account questions and a model routing institutional orders are not the same risk, and a flat rule would either strangle the first or under-police the second.

groups.heading: What would prove the speech wrong

blocks.svg:
1. Speech or agenda. The chairman signals intent. Two of this article's four items are already past this step.
2. Consultation paper. The first hard test: a published proposal, with a public comment window.
3. Board approval. SEBI's board votes. The public markers are board-outcome press releases; agenda papers appear only after decisions.
4. Circular. The operative rule, with an effective date. Only this changes behaviour.
The standard SEBI rulemaking path, drawn for this article. The four items sit at different stations: the bond pilot is already live, the AI guidelines are between consultation and finalisation, and the short-selling review and graded compliance are at the start.

blocks.html: A SEBI idea travels a known road: signal, consultation paper, board approval, circular. The four items are not at the same station - the bond pilot is already running and the AI guidelines are past consultation - which is why the honest reading of this speech is not "reform is coming" but "reform is at different stations, and each station has an observable marker". The checklist, item by item:

Demat 2.0 moves to phase two if tokenised bonds start trading on the RFQ platforms, with the market-making framework the speech separately lists arriving alongside - and if the retail-access phase in the launch release follows. It stalls if issuance stops at three issuers and Rs 1,025 crore. The short-selling review is real if it ends in a published consultation paper on borrow costs and eligible stock - and a slogan if it ends in a committee that never surfaces. Graded compliance is real if the next broker-regulation consultation actually sorts obligations by scale, client exposure and technology reliance. The AI framework is real if the final guidelines land with the promised tiering and kill switches - and the sandbox moves from "exploring" to a dated pilot.

The markers to watch are public and dated: consultation papers, board-outcome press releases and circulars on SEBI's website - not board agenda papers, which SEBI has published only after decisions since its 2008 transparency rules. If none of the four produces a document over the next two board cycles, the correct reading of the ANMI speech is that it was a speech. If even two produce them, the correct reading is that the market's plumbing is about to be rebuilt - and the winners are the saver who gets a third asset, the small broker who gets to keep existing, and the sceptic who finally gets to borrow.
A speech that tells you where each item stands - and which document comes next - is rare. This one did. The consultation papers, board outcomes and circulars are where to grade it.

Source: Speech text, SEBI website (primary, read in full) / Demat 2.0 pilot launch release, 10 Sep (owning) / AI/ML consultation paper, June 2025 (owning) / Debt denomination circular, July 2024 (owning)

Claims about the speech come from the published speech text, read in full, on SEBI's website. The Demat 2.0 pilot status - three issuers, Rs 1,025 crore, first phase ongoing at launch, later phases via RFQ platforms and retail access - comes from SEBI's 10 September launch release. The AI rulemaking history is SEBI's June 2025 consultation paper. Retail bond denominations follow SEBI's July 2024 circular cutting privately placed debt to Rs 10,000. The Rs 61-lakh-crore corporate-bond figure is the chairman's, from the speech.
Slow Burn long read, Sunday 25 October 2026. The daily paper: "Three banks deliver, the Gulf bristles".

21.title: Slow Burn - The war premium
21.fact: 26 October 2026. What it now costs to insure a barrel of oil through the Strait of Hormuz - and why that price, set in a market most people never see, is inside everything from freight to your insurance renewals.
21.intro: One argument, told as a story: the largest cost of this war is not the oil price - it is the price of moving anything through where the war is.

blocks.html: Before this war, insuring a ship through the Gulf cost 0.15 to 0.25 percent of the ship's value per trip. In mid-October the quote was 6 to 10 percent.

Picture the decision in front of a shipowner this week - an illustrative case, built from the market's actual numbers. His vessel is a very large crude carrier, worth perhaps $100 million, chartered to lift two million barrels from the Gulf. To sail, he needs additional war-risk cover - the market calls it an additional premium, or AP - because the Strait of Hormuz sits on the London market's list of conflict-risk waters. Before 28 February, when this war began, that AP would have cost him about a quarter of one percent of hull value: $250,000, a line item. At the mid-October quotes of 6 to 10 percent, the same transit costs $6 to $10 million. Per trip. On a two-million-barrel cargo that is $3 to $5 a barrel from the rate quotes alone; one researcher's arithmetic, on a costlier hull, puts the insurance line at about $6 a barrel at the mid-point - against 11 to 19 cents before the war (Driss Effina's cost-build note, 24 Oct; the per-barrel figures are his model, the rate quotes are the market's). At those prices, the insurance on one voyage can cost more than the ship earns on several ordinary voyages. Some owners, brokers say, simply wait at anchor for the quote to drift down. Some always do.

groups.heading: The year the map caught fire

blocks.html: The premium's path this year is a diary of the war itself. Before 28 February: 0.15 to 0.25 percent, a price so routine it barely had a news cycle. Within weeks of the war's start - Iran's moves of early March were described by the US Energy Information Administration as an effective closure of the strait - quotes ran between 1 and 10 percent, and underwriters cut their quotes' validity from 24 hours to 12. An April ceasefire produced a lull. A US-Iran memorandum of understanding signed on 17 June brought Gulf APs down to about 2 percent - the market believed it. Then attacks in early July broke the calm, and by 22 July the benchmark voice of the market, Marcus Baker, global head of marine, cargo and logistics at the broker Marsh, was telling S&P Global Platts that Hormuz rates had jumped from 1-3 percent to 7.5-10 percent of hull value (S&P Global, 22 July). The memorandum expired in August; rates eased to a 3-8 percent band anyway. Renewed strikes from 2 September brought the corridor back to active conflict, and mid-October quotes stand at 6-10 percent, forty times the peacetime price.

items.title: Before 28 Feb 2026
items.detail: Gulf war-risk AP: 0.15-0.25% of hull value per transit. About 130-135 Hormuz crossings a day.

items.title: March 2026
items.detail: War begins; EIA calls Iran's moves an effective closure. APs requote at 1-10%; quote validity cut from 24 to 12 hours.

items.title: 17 Jun 2026
items.detail: US-Iran memorandum signed. APs fall to about 2% - the market prices peace.

items.title: 22 Jul 2026
items.detail: Marsh: rates back to 7.5-10% after early-July attacks. Only 10 transits on 21 July, against 16 the day before.

items.title: Aug 2026
items.detail: Memorandum expires; APs 3-8%. Strikes resume 2 September.

items.title: Mid-Oct 2026
items.detail: APs quoted 6-10%. Windward counts 13 crossings on 4 Oct. Crude flows 8.5m barrels a day in the week to 12 Oct, against about 15m pre-war.

groups.heading: How the price is actually made

blocks.html: The war-risk market is small, London-centred, and built so that cover never truly disappears - it reprices. Three mechanics carry the story. First, the list: the Lloyd's Joint War Committee, a committee of underwriters, designates the waters where ordinary hull cover stops applying and APs begin; the Gulf, the Red Sea and the Black Sea all sit on that register now, the first time in the careers of working underwriters that so many major chokepoints have been listed at once. "We haven't had anything to this large of a degree since World War II," Charlie McCammon, senior director of marine North America at WTW, told the firm's October market briefing (WTW's Q3 marine briefing, 16 Oct). Second, the notice: when risk jumps, insurers do not cancel - under the standard institute clauses they give notice, typically seven days, and reinstate cover at revised areas and rates. A ship mid-voyage keeps its cover; the next voyage pays the new price. Third, the club: war risks are placed across many underwriters on common terms - a subscription market - so a rate is less a single firm's opinion than the market's clearing level, agreed risk by risk.

The fourth mechanic is the one that reaches calm waters. The reinsurance capacity behind all war-risk cover is one shared pool of capital across theatres. "If you have repeated losses in one theater, that could reduce global capacity, driving up baseline pricing everywhere else," McCammon said. A Red Sea underwriter who has never insured a Gulf transit still pays for Gulf losses. And the losses are arriving: the reinsurance broker Howden Re has estimated claims of $2 to $3 billion in war and political-violence lines, against annual premiums of $1.5 to $2 billion (Effina's note, citing Howden Re). Losses that thick change renewal negotiations for every marine book on earth - including books with no Gulf exposure at all.

Yet the market functions. Baker, in July, put global hull war capacity at $2.5 to $3 billion against a typical Gulf vessel value under $100 million - cover could theoretically be placed 25 times over. The constraint is not capacity but nerve: after a cluster of attacks, underwriters simply pause quoting for 24 to 48 hours until the picture clears, James Reason, WTW's head of hull for marine GB, explained: "There is still elements of competition, albeit it's still quite cautious at times, but it is functioning." His marker for a true market break: not these losses, but a single event that trapped a fleet - "if we had all of the tonnage that was trapped or blocked in the Straits of Hormuz... then that starts to move the dial and then becomes a reinsurance event."

The bill does not stop at the shipowner. Gulf-to-Far East crude freight went from $1.73 a barrel in January to about $33 in October; spot earnings for a VLCC - the two-million-barrel class - hit $805,000 a day on 9 October, 27 times January's benchmark (Effina, citing Clarksons-derived figures). The International Maritime Organization has recorded 106 confirmed incidents and 24 seafarer deaths since February. And the traffic tells the real story: from 130-135 transits a day before the war to 13 on 4 October - a strait that carries a fifth of the world's petroleum liquids running at a tenth of its traffic, as an armed corridor with naval escorts. US Central Command said this weekend its forces have shepherded more than 3,000 commercial vessels through in six months.

For India the arithmetic is direct. Every dollar on crude adds about $2 billion a year to the import bill - and layered on the oil price itself is this second, quieter tax: war cover at forty times its peacetime rate, freight at nineteen times, and a reinsurance renewal season that will price this year's $2-3 billion of claims into every war and political-violence treaty the industry signs. If you work in insurance, this is the rare week the war's most important number is not on a screen of oil prices - it is in a quote valid for twelve hours, from a market that prices danger before headlines do.

groups.heading: What would bring it down - and what would prove this reading wrong

blocks.html: Twice this year the premium has fallen: after April's ceasefire and after June's memorandum, when APs touched 2 percent. Both lulls broke on events, not words. The markers that would actually reprice the Gulf: a named, dated US-Iran framework - the Qatari channel now open in Tehran is the first candidate - holding long enough for transits to rebuild toward 30 a day; the Joint War Committee delisting or de-escalating the area, which it does on evidence, not sentiment; and claims staying inside the market's appetite rather than producing Reason's fleet-loss event. The reading in this piece is wrong if rates collapse toward 2 percent while the attacks continue - meaning capacity, not risk, was the real driver - or if the premium proves a weeks-long spike that the next month erases, in which case the war premium was a headline, not a repricing. Forty years ago, in the tanker war of the 1980s this one now resembles, Lloyd's opened on Saturday mornings to write the business (Marsh's Marcus Baker, in the S&P interview). The market always stays open. The price is the message.

Slow Burn long reads. "The war premium": reported from S&P Global Platts' July interview with Marsh's Marcus Baker, WTW's October marine briefing, and Driss Effina's sourced cost-build note of 24 October; per-barrel model figures are the author's own, as labelled.

22.title: The company that said no
22.fact: A Slow Burn long read, Tuesday 27 October 2026. Anthropic - five years old, maker of Claude - filed on Monday to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, weeks after a federal appeals court ruled the Pentagon could keep calling it a supply-chain risk. This is how a walkout from OpenAI became the most valuable AI company ever to ask the public for money.
22.intro: The story in one line: a brother and sister left the world's most famous AI lab over what it was becoming, built the self-consciously careful rival, and discovered that the carefulness would be tested by customers far bigger than any benchmark - including the United States government. Every claim below comes from the sources listed at the end; where two accounts differ, the difference is named.

blocks.html: On Monday, 26 October 2026, Anthropic, PBC filed its Form S-1 with the US Securities and Exchange Commission - the registration document a company must publish before selling shares to the public. It plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, and the debut is targeted for Thanksgiving week (CNBC's live coverage of the filing). The company had filed confidentially in June, letting the SEC review its numbers away from the public; Monday's document is the version investors will price.

What the document shows, by the numbers reported from it: revenue of $41 million in 2023, $4.6 billion in 2025, and $16.3 billion in the first six months of 2026 alone. And then the other line: a net loss of $80.7 billion for that same half - the largest loss any IPO filer has ever presented - which the coverage attributes mostly to accounting charges, the non-cash revaluation of the company's own funding instruments as its private valuation soared. The 2025 loss was $42 billion on the same basis (Fortune's read of the filing; Kepler's S-1 breakdown).

A five-year-old company went from $41 million to a $16.3 billion half-year - and booked the biggest paper loss in IPO history on the way. Both lines are the same story: value re-rating faster than any business in memory.

blocks.label: Anthropic revenue, $ billions (2026 figure is the first six months only); source: Kepler S-1 breakdown

blocks.html: If the listing holds its timing, Anthropic will reach the public market before OpenAI - the company its founders left, and the rival every line of its story is measured against.

Dario Amodei spent five years at OpenAI and ran its research - the teams behind GPT-2 and GPT-3. His sister Daniela ran safety and policy there. By the end of 2020, both had decided the lab was becoming something they could not sign their names to: Microsoft's billion dollars had arrived, a for-profit arm was being built, and the people whose job was to ask whether the systems were safe were losing the argument to the people whose job was to ship them. They quit quietly - no open letter, no public campaign (Fortune's 2023 interview with Dario Amodei: "why I quit OpenAI").

Eleven OpenAI employees left in all (AI Business's contemporary account). In May 2021 the group surfaced as Anthropic - the Amodeis plus five other senior OpenAI researchers, Jared Kaplan and Chris Olah among them - announcing itself with $124 million in Series A funding and a mission stated as a constraint: build reliable, steerable AI systems, or do not build them (TechCrunch, 28 May 2021; Anthropic's own announcement). The company incorporated as a public-benefit corporation - a legal form that obliges the board to weigh a stated public purpose alongside profit. The belief, as its later court filing put it, was that AI "should be developed and used in a way that" maximizes safety - and the bet was that customers would pay for exactly that.

The bet had a shape most outsiders missed at the time. OpenAI would chase consumers; Anthropic would sell to enterprises - banks, drug companies, law firms - the buyers for whom a model doing something unpredictable is not embarrassing but uninsurable. Safety was not the marketing department. Safety was the sales pitch.

The product of that pitch was Claude. By June 2023 the chatbot was newly public and the company was positioning it as the dependable option: the model that says no more often and hallucinates less, aimed at professional work. The technical signature was "constitutional AI" - training the system against an explicit written set of principles rather than only against human raters' preferences, so that its refusals and cautions come from a document anyone can read.

Then the releases that made the revenue line: on 24 February 2025, Anthropic announced Claude 3.7 Sonnet alongside Claude Code, a programming agent that works inside a developer's own tools (Anthropic's announcements). Claude Code became the wedge the S-1 attributes the company's 2026 acceleration to - enterprises buying it by the seat. On 9 June 2026 came the flagship models Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5. Two months later the company was the most highly valued private AI firm in the world: on 28 May 2026 it raised $65 billion in a Series H round at a $965 billion post-money valuation, co-led by Altimeter - above OpenAI's own mark (Reuters; TechCrunch; Anthropic's announcement).

The money came with patrons who are also competitors. Google committed up to $40 billion over time (Reuters, 24 April 2026). Amazon, Anthropic's cloud partner, put $5 billion into the May round as part of a prior commitment (Business Standard) - having backed the company since 2023. The arrangement bought compute and credibility, and it mortgaged independence: Anthropic's two largest backers sell rival AI services, a tension the S-1 itself has to list among its risks.

In July 2025, the US Department of Defense awarded Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and xAI contracts worth up to $200 million each, to put frontier AI into intelligence analysis, planning and cyber operations. Claude went to work inside the national-security state. This account of what followed is from the Congressional Research Service's report of 5 October 2026 (CRS IN12669), which drew on the court record and contemporaneous reporting.

In January 2026, US forces captured Venezuela's president, Nicolás Maduro. Reporting indicated Claude had been used in the operation. Anthropic inquired about how the Defense Department was using its model - and the inquiry itself set off alarms inside the Pentagon: if the vendor disapproved of a use case, the vendor might one day switch the model off. The department asked Anthropic, as it asked other AI companies, to allow use of its models for "all lawful purposes". Anthropic said it was willing to adapt its usage policies for the Pentagon - except for two things it would not permit: mass domestic surveillance, and fully autonomous weapons. Dario Amodei explained the refusal in terms of capability, not pacifism: autonomous weapon systems "may prove critical for our national defense. But today, frontier AI systems are simply not reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons."

On 27 February 2026, President Trump directed federal agencies to "IMMEDIATELY CEASE all use" of Anthropic's technology. Days later, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk to national security - a label normally reserved for foreign adversaries' vendors - and barred defense contractors from working with the company at all. On 9 March, Anthropic sued, in two courts at once: a civil complaint in California and a petition in the DC Circuit.

On 27 August, the district court ruled for the company: the designation "violated the governing statutory scheme", was "arbitrary and capricious", and constituted "unlawful retaliation in violation of the First Amendment". It vacated the designation. On 25 September, a three-judge appeals panel reversed course - two judges to one - holding that the department had "ample support" for treating Claude's presence in its systems as a covered risk and that Anthropic's constitutional claims were "without merit". The ban stands while the company, in its own words, is "considering all options, including further review".
The moment Anthropic's founding creed stopped being a sales pitch: it told its largest potential customer that some uses were not for sale - and the customer tried to make an example of it.

groups.heading: 5. What made it work - and what it got wrong

blocks.html: What made it work is visible in the filing. First, the enterprise wedge: selling dependability to buyers who cannot tolerate surprise produced a revenue slope - $41 million, to $4.6 billion, to $16.3 billion in a half - that consumer subscriptions alone rarely generate. Second, the coding agent: Claude Code turned a chat product into a workflow tool companies build around, and the S-1 credits it for the 2026 acceleration. Third, timing the safety brand to the moment institutions began fearing the technology - the same positioning that made Anthropic a political target made it the default shortlist for regulated industries.

What it got wrong, or nearly did. It built on capital and compute from two patrons - Google and Amazon - that field competing models; dependence on a rival's cloud is a strategic debt that does not appear as a single line item. It assumed a written principles document and a benefit-corporation charter would insulate it from politics; the Pentagon episode showed a government can simply relabel a supplier as a risk, and that a court win can be reversed ninety days later. And it let the "safety company" frame harden into a public identity that critics could cast as the company claiming veto power over how the state defends itself. The lesson is not that the principles were wrong; the S-1's revenue suggests they were the product. The lesson is that principles marketed loudly become a target painted precisely.

groups.heading: 6. What would prove this story wrong

blocks.html: Three tests now run in public. The listing itself: if ANT prices weakly or breaks its issue price in the first weeks, the market is saying the revenue slope does not pay for the compute bill - the charge that Anthropic's growth is bought with someone else's capital at someone's else's price. The appeals path: if the supply-chain designation survives to become settled law, every government contract in the company's pipeline re-prices. And the rival: OpenAI's own filing is now a matter of when, and two audited AI balance sheets will invite a direct comparison only one of them can win. A year from now, this story reads either as the founding of the enterprise-AI era's first public company, or as the moment the safety premium met its price.

23.title: The company that lost its bank
23.fact: A Slow Burn long read, Wednesday 28 October 2026. On Monday, Paytm's parent One97 Communications reported a profit of Rs 225 crore for the September quarter - more than ten times the year-ago figure - nearly three years after the Reserve Bank of India shut down the bank at the centre of its business. This is the story of India's biggest IPO, <Fix>one</Fix> <Fix>of</Fix> its worst <Fix>debuts,</Fix> the order that took the bank away, and the rebuild that followed.
23.intro: The story in one line: the company that rode demonetisation to a record-breaking listing discovered its licence to operate was its real product, lost a large part of it in a single regulatory order, and survived by shrinking to the part of the business that earned money. Every claim below comes from the sources listed at the end; where two accounts differ, the difference is named.

groups.heading: 1. The wallet that won a demonetisation

blocks.html: Vijay Shekhar Sharma founded One97 Communications in 2000, a mobile-content company in the pre-smartphone era, and launched the Paytm wallet in 2010 - a way to keep a small balance on the phone and spend it without a card (dates from One97's 2021 IPO prospectus). For six years it was a useful product in a cash country. Then, on 8 November 2016, the government withdrew the two largest currency notes overnight, and queues formed at every ATM in India. Paytm did not need a queue: it was already in the phone. Merchants taped its QR code to counters because the alternative was turning customers away. Reuters covered the surge at the time - the wallet's user count and merchant base multiplied within weeks, and "Paytm" became a verb for paying by phone in the way "Google" had become a verb for search.

The pattern that decade set mattered later. Paytm grew by riding state-built rails and state-driven shocks: cheap smartphones, the Aadhaar identity system, and then UPI - the Unified Payments Interface, the central-bank-backed network that lets any bank account pay any other instantly, free. UPI made paying by phone universal, but it also made the wallet's stored balance less necessary. Paytm's answer was to spread outward: movie tickets, insurance, gold, lending - and a bank of its own.

In November 2021, at the peak of India's pandemic market boom, One97 Communications sold shares to the public. The numbers were records: Rs 18,300 crore raised at Rs 2,150 a share, the largest IPO India had ever seen. The bankers priced it for perfection - a company that had never posted a full-year profit, valued on the certainty that it would become the payment layer of a billion-person economy.

On listing day, 18 November 2021, the stock fell 27% - one of the worst major debuts in Indian market history, erasing roughly $5 billion of value in a session. Sharma, who had wept with joy at the morning's listing ceremony, told Reuters by the end of it: "One day does not decide what our future is." He was right, though not in the direction he meant. The stock would spend the next two years falling, and the worst day was not the first one.
The market's verdict on day one was about price. The verdict that mattered arrived later, and it was about permission.

blocks.alt: Abstract illustration of one very large cracked navy circle shedding small falling fragments
blocks.caption: The listing: the biggest circle in the room, with the crack already showing.

blocks.html: Paytm Payments Bank was the piece that made Paytm more than an app. A payments bank is a stripped-down Indian bank licence: it can take deposits and run payment accounts, but cannot lend. It held the wallets, the nodal accounts through which merchant settlements flowed, and a large share of the plumbing that made Paytm's QR codes and soundboxes - the little speakers that call out "Paytm par Rs 50 prapt hue" at lakhs of shop counters - actually work.

The regulator's discomfort built in stages. On 11 March 2022, the Reserve Bank of India barred Paytm Payments Bank from onboarding new customers and ordered an external audit of its IT systems - the kind of action the RBI takes when it stops trusting what a regulated entity tells it. The audit happened. So did a compliance validation exercise. What they found, the RBI would later say, was not fixed.

On 31 January 2024, the RBI published an order that was two pages long and ended Paytm Payments Bank as a going concern. After a system audit and compliance validation by external auditors, the bank was found to have "persistent non-compliances and continued material supervisory concerns". No deposits, credits, or top-ups into any customer account, wallet, or instrument after 29 February 2024. The nodal accounts of One97 Communications and Paytm Payments Services - the settlement pipes - were to be terminated by the same date. Whatever was already in the settlement pipeline had to be cleared by 15 March.

Read it again as a shopkeeper: the soundbox on the counter, the QR code on the wall, the wallet on the customer's phone - all of them drained into accounts the regulator had just ordered closed, with one month's notice. Paytm the app was not banned. But the bank under Paytm the app was gone.

blocks.alt: Abstract illustration of a crowd of small navy squares dammed against a tall rust wall with one narrow gate
blocks.caption: The order: one regulator's wall across the payment flow, with a single narrow gate.

blocks.html: The market's answer came in instalments, because the stock kept hitting its daily lower circuit - the exchange's automatic brake that stops a share from falling further that day. Over three sessions the stock fell 42%, erasing nearly Rs 20,500 crore of market value (Business Standard, 5 February 2024). The Enforcement Directorate reportedly questioned executives (moneycontrol's reporting at the time). On 16 February 2024, the stock touched Rs 318.05 intraday - its record low, 85% below the IPO price of twenty-seven months earlier (moneycontrol).

What was being priced was not a bad quarter. It was the possibility that the franchise itself - the merchants, the soundboxes, the habit of paying with Paytm - would migrate away while the company rebuilt its plumbing, and that what remained would be a wallet app in a country that had moved to UPI.

groups.heading: 6. The ten days, and the rebuild

blocks.html: The decision that saved the company was made in the days after the order, and it was unglamorous: move everything, bank by bank. Paytm's UPI handles - the @paytm addresses customers typed - had to live at other banks, and by March 2024 they did, migrated to four partner banks: the State Bank of India, HDFC Bank, Axis Bank and Yes Bank, after approval from NPCI, the body that runs UPI (company filing). The RBI itself published a consumer FAQ confirming the mechanics: Paytm QR codes and soundboxes would keep working only where merchants migrated to the partner banks' handles (Inc42's account of the FAQ). On 22 October 2024 came the formal unlock: NPCI granted Paytm third-party application provider status - permission, as a standalone app without its own bank, to onboard new UPI users again (company disclosure; The Hindu).

Then the company shrank on purpose. Out went the everything-app sprawl; in came a focus on the merchants who paid rather than the users who did not - subscription soundboxes and card machines, payment services, and loans distributed to merchants, with costs cut hard, including what the company describes as AI-led automation. The first proof arrived in July 2025: Paytm's first-ever profitable quarter, Rs 122.5 crore of profit after tax in Q1 FY26 (Business Standard). The second quarter of that year dipped back to Rs 21 crore - a figure that still included government payment-infrastructure incentives the company stopped receiving in December 2025. Then the rebuild found its level: Rs 225 crore in Q3 FY26, Rs 183.5 crore in Q4 FY26, Rs 220 crore in Q1 FY27, and Rs 225 crore in the quarter reported Monday - the sixth straight profitable quarter - more than ten times the year-ago figure, on revenue up 28% to Rs 2,648 crore, with 1.64 crore merchant devices installed and EBITDA up 90% to Rs 270 crore (the company's own earnings release, read in full).

Sharma had said it before it happened. At Davos in January 2025, with the stock still a fraction of the issue price, he told moneycontrol the UPI share was "easily recoverable" and the company would be PAT-profitable in some quarters. At ET's Global Business Summit weeks later, he put the stake in the ground personally: "I consider Paytm like my daughter." The first prediction has now printed twice.
Paytm lost the bank and kept the counter. The QR code on the wall never moved; only the account behind it did.
