blocks.caption: The rebuild: smaller blocks, but they stack.

blocks.html: There is one more turn, and it arrived six weeks ago. For years Paytm's argument with India's payments economics was that free UPI meant nobody who built the acceptance side got paid - the merchant soundboxes, the QR stickers, the settlement files. On 15 September 2026, the finance ministry published an FAQ setting a merchant discount rate - MDR, the fee a merchant pays per transaction - of 0.4% on person-to-merchant UPI payments above Rs 2,000, capped at Rs 300, effective 15 October; transactions up to Rs 2,000 stay free. NPCI then deferred the start, and Paytm's release says implementation follows immediately after Diwali, on a date to be notified, and estimates the uplift at about 2.5 basis points of payment processing margin on its current mix - with the caveat that the outcome takes two to three quarters to stabilise. Its own line in the release is the honest one: any MDR on UPI would be an upside, not the foundation.

groups.heading: 8. What made it work - and what it got wrong

blocks.html: What made it work is visible in the rebuild. First, the franchise was at the merchant counter, not in the bank: soundboxes and QR codes are physical, habitual, and painful to rip out, and competitors would have had to visit lakhs of shops one by one to take them. Second, the partner-bank migration was executed in weeks under deadline pressure with the regulator's own FAQ guiding customers - an operational march the company has never really been credited for. Third, the discipline arrived late but real: cutting to the monetisable core produced profit within six quarters of the worst day.

What it got wrong, or nearly did. It treated compliance as a backlog item while operating as critical national payment infrastructure - the RBI's finding of persistent non-compliance came after years of warnings, an audit, and a validation exercise. It let the app sprawl into everything while the core economics of free UPI stayed unsolved. And it priced the 2021 IPO for a certainty that had not been earned, which is why the debut did the damage it did. The lesson is not that ambition was wrong; the merchant network is the proof it was not. The lesson is that in a regulated business, the licence is the product.

groups.heading: 9. What would prove this story wrong

blocks.html: Three tests now run in public. The MDR test: if the implemented rates or exemptions land below the company's 2.5-basis-point estimate after the two-to-three-quarter stabilisation it names, the tailwind chapter of this story was oversold. The regulatory test: the Enforcement Directorate matter's public status remains unresolved, and a second action of the 2024 kind - against the surviving business this time - is the one event the rebuild cannot absorb twice. And the market-share test: PhonePe and Google Pay still carry most UPI volume, and if Paytm's merchant GMV share erodes while the big two stay free for consumers, the counter franchise proves weaker than the crash priced in. A year from now, this story reads either as the great Indian fintech survival, or as a company that survived the regulator only to be worn down by the duopoly.

24.title: The company that gave the internet away
24.fact: A Slow Burn long read, Thursday 29 October 2026. On Wednesday, Jio Platforms closed its first day of trading at Rs 1,419 a share, up 26.81% on its issue price, valued at Rs 13.05 lakh crore - instantly India's second-most-valuable listed company, ahead of Bharti Airtel. This is the story of how a free-data giveaway in 2016 became the largest public listing India has ever seen.
24.intro: The story in one line: a company that could afford to give its product away did exactly that, built the largest subscriber base in the country while rivals priced by the gigabyte, cleaned its balance sheet in one fifty-eight-day sprint, and arrived at the stock market a decade later with the debt gone and the customers already inside. Every claim below comes from the sources listed at the end, most of them the company's own releases.

blocks.html: Wednesday morning at the National Stock Exchange, the Ambani family assembled for a listing ceremony that had been expected, on and off, for well over a year. Mukesh Ambani stood with Nita Ambani, Isha Ambani and Anant Ambani; Akash Ambani, Jio Platforms' managing director, spoke; NSE's chief executive Ashishkumar Chauhan attended (Indian Express). The stock opened at Rs 1,358, a premium of 21.36% to the issue price of Rs 1,119, and closed at Rs 1,419 - up Rs 300, or 26.81%, on the day (Fortune India; Indian Express).

By the close, Jio Platforms was worth Rs 13.05 lakh crore - more than Bharti Airtel's Rs 12.16 lakh crore, behind only its own parent, Reliance Industries, at about Rs 15.67 lakh crore. The issue itself had already set its records before a single trade: Rs 30,213 crore raised, the largest IPO in Indian history, passing Hyundai Motor India's Rs 27,870 crore from 2024; about 1.37 crore applications, the first Indian IPO to cross one crore; subscribed 22.19 times overall. One brokerage note captured the day's strangeness flatly: Motilal Oswal initiated coverage that morning with a Buy - and a target price of Rs 1,350, below the price the market closed at. The company debuted, in other words, above at least one major broker's idea of what it is worth.
A 22-times-subscribed book and a first-day pop mean the optimistic case was paid for in advance. What buyers own now is the ten years that produced this room.

To understand the launch, hold the 2016 market in mind: mobile data in India was sold by the gigabyte at prices that made streaming a luxury, and most of the country rationed the internet like a metered utility. On 1 September 2016, Reliance Jio Infocomm filed its tariff plans with the regulator and announced what it called the Jio Welcome Offer (company release, read in full): from 5 September, users would get unlimited LTE data, national voice, video and messaging - free of cost - until 31 December 2016.

The mechanism was brutal in its simplicity. The barrier to India's internet was never demand; it was the price of the marginal megabyte. Jio made the marginal megabyte zero and let the habit form. Free service - the Welcome Offer to 31 December 2016, extended by the Happy New Year Offer to 31 March 2017 (company release, 1 December 2016) - was not a discount; it was an invitation to reorganise daily life around data: video calls, films, payments, all of it, before the first bill ever arrived. Competitors pricing by the gigabyte were suddenly selling a metered product next to an unmetered one.

blocks.alt: Abstract illustration of a crowd of small navy squares pressed against a tall rust wall with one narrow gate
blocks.caption: 2016: data behind a price wall, with one narrow gate. The Welcome Offer took the wall down; the Happy New Year Offer kept it down to 31 March 2017.

blocks.html: On 21 February 2017, Mukesh Ambani addressed what he called "my 100 million Jio customers" (the chairman's speech, in full): "Jio launched its services on Sept 5th of last year. Today... just 170 days later... Jio has crossed the 100 million customer mark." One hundred million people in under six months - an adoption pace with no precedent in Indian consumer business, built on the free offer and the habit it created.

The free period ended on 31 March 2017; the customers stayed and, with Jio Prime from April, started paying. The number that tracks that conversion is ARPU - average revenue per user, the monthly rupee yield of one subscriber. Jio's ARPU was Rs 181.7 in FY24, Rs 214 in FY26, and Rs 215.6 in the April-June quarter of FY27 (Indian Express, from the company's disclosures). Bharti Airtel's, for comparison, stood at Rs 264. Jio won the subscribers; the industry kept a price umbrella over its head that it is still, a decade later, climbing toward.

blocks.html: Building a nationwide 4G network from nothing had been funded the way everything at Reliance was funded: with debt. By 31 March 2020, the group carried net debt of Rs 161,035 crore (company release, 19 June 2020). What happened next, in the middle of a national lockdown, unwound that debt in fifty-eight days.

It began on 22 April 2020: Facebook invested Rs 43,574 crore for a 9.99% stake in Jio Platforms (company release) - the largest foreign direct investment for a minority stake in India, the release noted. Then the queue formed. Over the following weeks: Silver Lake, Vista Equity Partners, General Atlantic, KKR, Mubadala, ADIA, TPG, L Catterton and Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund. By 19 June - fifty-eight days after the Facebook announcement - Jio Platforms had raised Rs 115,693.95 crore from ten global investors, and a parallel Reliance rights issue had raised Rs 53,124.20 crore more: Rs 168,818 crore in all. The company's own release stated the result in one line: "RIL has become NET DEBT-FREE." On 15 July, Google closed the round with Rs 33,737 crore for 7.73% (company release), taking the equity raise to about Rs 1.52 lakh crore in three months (Intel Capital and Qualcomm Ventures also invested that July) - and putting both Facebook and Google on the shareholder register of the same Indian telecom company.

The 2020 spree did two things at once: it erased the debt that built the network, and it priced the network's owner in front of the world's most demanding investors - six years before the public got its turn.

The asset that listed on Wednesday is no longer a SIM card business. From the parent's Q1 FY27 presentation of July 2026 (read in full): Jio Platforms' quarterly revenue was Rs 45,961 crore, up 12% year on year; EBITDA Rs 20,865 crore, up 15.1%. The subscriber base stood above 533 million, with 285 million of them on its 5G network - a network the company says is built on proprietary technology. In homes, it counted 28.6 million fixed-broadband subscribers, about half on Jio AirFiber, its fixed-wireless product, where it claims over 78% of the Indian market. Digital services - cloud, enterprise connectivity, IoT, managed services - grew 20% year on year.

blocks.alt: Abstract illustration of navy, ochre and rust blocks assembling into a rising staircase
blocks.caption: Connectivity first, then homes, then cloud and enterprise: smaller blocks, stacked in order.

blocks.html: The listing was first announced in mid-2025 (Indian Express) and took more than a year to arrive. The offer, when it came, was structured plainly: a price band of Rs 1,065 to Rs 1,119, an entirely fresh issue of about 27 crore shares - no promoter selling a single one, so every rupee of the Rs 30,213 crore goes to the company. Anchor investors were brought in first, for Rs 8,110 crore, with mutual funds taking over a third of the institutional anchor allocation. Employees got a reserved slice of 46,94,835 shares at a Rs 54 discount to the price. When the book closed on 23 October, the institutional portion was subscribed nearly 71 times, non-institutional about 14 times, retail 2.72 times: 22.19 times overall, with bids for 438.26 crore shares against 19.75 crore on offer to the public.

The offer documents name two uses: up to Rs 27,500 crore to repay borrowings of the operating subsidiary Reliance Jio Infocomm - the 2020 deleveraging, completed a second time from the inside - and the rest for general corporate purposes. Around the raise sits a commercial calendar: Nomura expects an industry-wide tariff hike of about 15% around November-December, the recurring event that has driven every step of the ARPU chart above. And there is the ambition Akash Ambani stated at the ceremony: "In our first 10 years, we democratised data... In our next 10, we want to democratise every technology that can transform Indian lives: AI, cloud, connected devices, connectivity even from space." Meta still holds about 10% of the company and Google about 8% - the AI partnerships the market is pricing sit inside the shareholding itself.

groups.heading: 8. What made it work - and what it got wrong

blocks.html: What worked, in order: the free offer converted the country's internet from a rationed utility to a daily habit before anyone was billed; the parent absorbed a decade of capital expenditure that no standalone rival could have carried; the 2020 sprint removed the debt exactly when the world was offering cheap equity; and the platform was stacked on the pipe - homes, cloud, enterprise - so that connectivity's thin margins were never the whole business. The honest list of what it got wrong, or has not yet gotten right: ARPU still sits about 18% below Airtel's, the price umbrella it created has not fully closed; the AI and cloud build-out repeats the original wager - spend first, monetise later - in a market where the payoff is less proven than connectivity was; and the stock debuted above at least one major broker's target, which means the public buyer starts where the easy optimism is already spent.

groups.heading: 9. What would prove this story wrong

blocks.html: Three tests now run in public. The ARPU test: if Jio's ARPU stalls below roughly Rs 220 through FY27 while Airtel's keeps climbing, the umbrella is closing the wrong way and the volume story has no price story to hold it. The tariff test: if the expected November-December hike slips past the first quarter of 2027, the regulator and the market are signalling the ceiling has been reached - and the monetisation chapter of this story was oversold. And the platform test: if digital-services growth - 20% in the last presentation - slows to connectivity's 11% (the last presentation's figure) before the AI partnerships produce a visible revenue line, the platform stacked on the pipe is a brochure, and the company is a utility with a glamorous register. A decade from now, this reads either as the great Indian consumer-internet build, or as the most expensive entry price retail investors ever paid for a telecom.

25.title: Reading Earth in a hundred colours
25.fact: A Slow Burn long read, Friday 30 October 2026. On Thursday, Pixxel - the Bengaluru-founded hyperspectral satellite company - announced Pixxel Federal, a US subsidiary for American government missions, led by a former National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency veteran. Seven weeks earlier it had closed a $100-million round, the largest ever for an Indian space startup. This is the story of how two twenty-year-olds with no money got here.
25.intro: The story in one line: two BITS Pilani students decided the planet needed a health monitor, survived a public launch scrub that would have ended most startups, flew their own satellites anyway, and converted flown hardware into NASA and NRO contracts and a $195-million war chest - because in this business, governments buy what is already in orbit. Every claim below comes from the sources listed at the end.

blocks.html: Thursday's announcement was short and precise (company release, read in full): Pixxel has established Pixxel Federal, a US subsidiary that will sell Earth observation, satellite systems and geospatial intelligence to American federal customers - civilian, defence and intelligence agencies. Its chief executive is Allyson Jenkins, who joined Pixxel in January 2025 as vice president for the public sector after nine years at the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, the US agency that analyses satellite imagery for the government. Three board members were named alongside her, including a retired US Army lieutenant general. The subsidiary will open an office in the Washington, DC area.

A foreign-founded startup setting up a dedicated American federal arm is a familiar move in one industry above all: defence and intelligence space. It is how a company tells the world's largest buyer of satellite data that it intends to be treated as an American supplier. What makes Pixxel's version striking is who is making it - a company founded by two twenty-year-old undergraduates in Pilani, Rajasthan, which today operates what it calls the world's highest-resolution commercial hyperspectral constellation, holds a NASA data contract and a National Reconnaissance Office contract, and has raised $195 million in total (Series C release, September 2026).

blocks.alt: Editorial illustration of Earth seen from orbit with a small satellite tracing a dotted path
blocks.caption: One small satellite, one dotted orbit. Pixxel's bet is that a hundred colours per pixel change what an orbit is worth.

blocks.html: Awais Ahmed and Kshitij Khandelwal started Pixxel in 2018 as twenty-year-old undergraduates at BITS Pilani (YourStory, May 2019; the company's own timeline begins in February 2019 - the building predates the paperwork). They had met building a Hyperloop pod - the team was among the finalists in SpaceX's 2017 competition - and an early mentor, Dileep Nath, helped shape the satellite idea: a health monitor for the planet. The fundraising was brutal. Ahmed has described the rejections plainly: nobody wanted to look at it - it was hardware, it was space hardware, and it was students (Hindu BusinessLine interview). The BITS Pilani network itself funded the early prototype work.

The company's own timeline marks how scrappy the start was: its first office - in Indiranagar, Bengaluru - opened only in January 2021, three years after they started building (Pixxel's About page). By then it had already survived the worst day of its young life.

A conventional satellite camera sees the way your phone does: a few broad bands of colour - red, green, blue, sometimes a handful more. That is multispectral imaging, typically three to ten bands. Hyperspectral imaging splits the incoming light into hundreds of narrow bands - Pixxel's first pathfinder captured more than 150 - and every material on Earth reflects light differently across those bands. A healthy wheat crop and a stressed one look identical in three bands and unmistakably different in a hundred and fifty. So do a mineral deposit and the rock around it, an oil slick and clean water, a camouflaged structure and the forest beside it.

That is the product: not pictures, but identification. Pixxel's Firefly satellites image at five-metre resolution across a forty-kilometre swath (Reuters, January 2025) - meaning each pixel covers a five-metre square of ground, each of them read in hundreds of colours. Agriculture, mining, oil and gas, environment monitoring and defence all buy versions of the same thing: knowing what is actually down there, before anyone visits.

blocks.alt: Editorial illustration of farmland divided into many thin strips of different muted colours, like a spectrum
blocks.caption: One field, a hundred wavelengths. Hyperspectral imaging reads each strip of land in far more colours than the eye or a phone camera can.

blocks.html: In February 2021, Pixxel's first satellite - Anand, named after a team member's grandfather - was days from flying as a secondary payload on ISRO's PSLV-C51. Around 10 February, the company discovered that a vendor had supplied erroneous reports on the testing status of critical components. Two days before the satellite was due to ship to Sriharikota, the founders withdrew it from the launch (the company's own retrospective; Indian Express Explained). For a startup whose entire pitch was hardware that flies, pulling its first satellite in public was the kind of event that ends companies.

What they did next defined them. Rather than wait months to requalify Anand, they diverted funding from their planned commercial satellite and built a second pathfinder from concept in about a year - they did not want, as the retrospective puts it, all their eggs in one basket satellite. Shakuntala launched on 1 April 2022 aboard SpaceX's Transporter-4 from Cape Canaveral, weighing under fifteen kilograms and reading more than 150 bands at ten-metre resolution - at the time the world's highest-resolution commercial hyperspectral satellite. It worked for 619 days in orbit. Anand itself finally flew on 26 November 2022, aboard ISRO's PSLV-C54 (company timeline). Around the Shakuntala launch, the company raised its Series A - $25 million by the launch-day release, $27 million with In-Q-Tel, the US intelligence community's venture arm, among investors by the company's own timeline - and counted over fifty customers who had signed pre-launch agreements.
The scrub was the making of the company: it chose rigor over schedule in public, then built a replacement satellite in a year. Every later contract rests on that choice being visible.

The scrub taught Pixxel the industry's central commercial fact, which Ahmed stated to Reuters in January 2025 (read in full): government agencies want to see things launched and working before committing. Demonstration satellites come first; contracts follow orbit. By then the company had about 65 clients signed ahead of its commercial constellation's launch, including Rio Tinto, BP and India's Ministry of Agriculture.

The Fireflies flew in two trios from Vandenberg: the first three aboard SpaceX's Transporter-12 on 14 January 2025, the second three on 26-27 August 2025 - completing a six-satellite first phase that Pixxel calls the world's highest-resolution commercial hyperspectral constellation, reading more than 135 bands at five-metre resolution with a 24-hour revisit. Satsearch's chief operations officer Narayan Prasad told Reuters the commissioning gave India more hyperspectral imaging capacity than ISRO itself - a watershed, in his word, for the country's private space sector. The Fireflies are the asset underneath everything announced since: the NASA Commercial SmallSat Data Acquisition contract, the NRO's Strategic Commercial Enhancements award of May 2026, and now Pixxel Federal.

blocks.alt: Editorial illustration of six small satellites spaced along a dotted ring around a two-tone Earth, linked to ground stations
blocks.caption: Six Fireflies in a ring: five-metre pixels, forty-kilometre swaths, a hundred-plus colours each.

blocks.svg: The market Pixxel sells into, US$ billions; satellite imagery plus analysis today, and the 2029 estimate (Ahmed, via Reuters Jan 2025)

blocks.html: On 7 September 2026, Pixxel announced a $100 million Series C, co-led by Temasek and Seraphim Space, with new investors 360 ONE and IMM Investment joining existing backers Radical Ventures, growX and M&G Catalyst (company release, read in full). Total funding: $195 million - the largest round ever raised by an Indian space-technology company.

The release names what the money builds: Honeybee, the next constellation, adding shortwave-infrared, synthetic-aperture radar and ultra-high-resolution optical imaging, with the first satellite planned for 2027; Aurora, the software platform that turns the imagery into analysis; and manufacturing across India and the United States. Around the round sit the institutional wins that justify it: the NASA and NRO contracts, iDEX defence-innovation wins in India, and the lead role in an IN-SPACe public-private partnership to build a twelve-satellite constellation for the Indian government.
The round is priced on a sequence, not a story: fly hardware, win government contracts, then raise. Pixxel ran the sequence in that order, which is why the cheque could be this size.

The context is a state project. India holds about 2% of the global space economy, and the government's target is to grow its space sector from $8 billion to $44 billion by 2030 (Reuters) - a five-fold expansion that presumes private companies like this one do the growing. Pixxel is not alone in the sky: Finland's Kuva Space and America's Orbital Sidekick chase the same hyperspectral buyers, and the biggest defence primes are paying attention to the same contracts Pixxel Federal now wants.

So the honest tests, dated and falsifiable. The Honeybee test: the first next-generation satellite is promised for 2027 - if it slips past that year, the $100 million bought time, not acceleration. The Washington test: Pixxel Federal is a structure, not revenue; if no named federal contract flows through it within a year of this week's announcement, the subsidiary was a brochure. And the market test: the $19-billion-by-2029 estimate is the company's own framing, quoted from its chief executive; if the hyperspectral slice stays a half-to-one-billion-dollar niche (Ahmed's own figure) while Kuva Space and Orbital Sidekick split it three ways, the constellation is real but the valuation is not. A decade from now, this reads either as the company that taught India to sell orbits to the world - or as the best-funded demonstration that governments buy slowly.

Read the company's own release first (Suzlon's Q2 statement, read in full) and the quarter is a record: 710 megawatts delivered, the most ever in a second quarter; revenue up 26% to Rs 4,869 crore; an order book past 6 gigawatts, about a year and a half of work; net worth crossing Rs 10,000 crore; a CRISIL upgrade to AA-. Then read the second headline: management cut its FY27 margin guidance from 17% to 15%, citing mix, commodity costs and currency, and on Friday the stock fell 8% to Rs 33.85. Brokers kept their buys - Investec at Rs 56, I-Sec at Rs 55, UBS at Rs 58 - and the market sold anyway.

That tension - a real recovery, punished for honesty - only makes sense against the company's history. Suzlon has been here before, on the other side: a story told bigger than the balance sheet. This time the balance sheet spoke first. The arc between those two postures is the story.

blocks.alt: Editorial illustration of modern wind turbines on a Gujarat ridge at dawn
blocks.caption: Twenty-two gigawatts installed across 17 countries, by the company's own count.

groups.heading: 2. Power cuts and a German turbine

blocks.html: In 1992, all of India had 42 megawatts of wind power (Suzlon's own history). Tulsi Tanti and his three brothers ran a textile business in Surat, Gujarat, and their problem was not the market for cloth - it was electricity. Power cuts interrupted production, and industrial tariffs ran at twice what American factories paid. Tanti's answer was to buy a German wind turbine for the mill. By the company's own telling, and the New York Times' 2006 account, it was a turbine they could not keep running.

Most mill owners would have sold the machine and gone back to diesel. Tanti concluded the machine was not the hard part - everything around it was: siting, installation, grid connection, maintenance. In 1995 he founded Suzlon with $600,000 raised by selling family property (Forbes' obituary of Tanti), installed its first 0.27-megawatt turbine within three months, and made the inconvenience the business model: Suzlon would do everything - research, manufacturing, installation, and decades of operations - so the customer only bought wind. India had 1,155 megawatts of wind by 2000.

blocks.alt: Editorial illustration of a 1990s Surat textile mill beside a small early wind turbine
blocks.caption: The mill came first; the turbine was meant to keep its looms running.

blocks.html: The climb was startlingly fast. Suzlon was not in the world top ten in 2002; by 2005 it had passed Siemens to become the world's fifth-largest wind-turbine maker by installed megawatts, and it listed on the Indian exchanges that year (the New York Times, September 2006, read in full). Tulsi Tanti was a billionaire by 2006; by 2007 the brothers were worth a combined $10 billion and Suzlon was the most valuable wind-turbine company on earth, with R&D in Germany, the Netherlands, Denmark and India, and four-fifths of its order book outside India.

The demand engine was a market failure turned into a market. Tanti told the Times that roughly 70% of the demand for wind turbines in India came from industrial users fleeing the grid - factories buying their own weather. The paper's reporter found the company's reach in villages like Khori, where a farmer named Patil watched turbines rise over his bean field, where thieves stripped the copper cables, and where 300-mile night convoys moved 110-foot blades. It was the frontier, and Suzlon owned it.

At the peak, Tanti spent the winnings on vertical control and global scale. Suzlon bought Hansen Transmissions, a Belgian gearbox maker, and then in 2007 won a hotly contested battle for REpower, a German turbine manufacturer, at a price of about $2 billion. The acquisitions were financed with debt - about Rs 100 billion that had to be refinanced by 2010. Then the world turned: a global glut cut turbine prices 23% from their 2009 peak, blade-quality reports hit the stock, and the losses ran three straight years.

The lesson is the oldest one in cyclical manufacturing: leverage taken at the top of a cycle is repaid at the bottom. Suzlon had bought the best assets in its industry at the worst possible moment, with money it had not yet earned.

On 11 October 2012, Suzlon defaulted on $209 million of foreign currency convertible bonds - the biggest convertible-bond default in Indian corporate history (contemporary report). A month later its lenders admitted the company to corporate debt restructuring: about Rs 11,000 crore recast, a two-year moratorium, repayment stretched over eight years, interest cut from about 14% to 11% (Mint's report on the CDR admission). Group net debt stood near Rs 13,000 crore. The shares had fallen 59% that year; they rose 10.7% to Rs 17.10 on the day the restructuring was announced, because survival had been priced out.
What carried Suzlon up - leverage plus ambition - is exactly what nearly killed it. The climb and the collapse were the same decision, taken twice.

blocks.alt: Editorial illustration of a lone wind turbine under a dark storm sky with dissolving chart bars
blocks.caption: 2012: India's biggest convertible-bond default, and a 59% fall in the share price in a single year.

groups.heading: 6. The white knight, and the sale of the jewels

blocks.html: The rescue, when it came, was unglamorous. In February 2015, Dilip Shanghvi - the founder of Sun Pharmaceutical and then India's richest man - put Rs 1,800 crore of his family's money into Suzlon for a 23% stake, with no change in management. Three months later, on 30 April 2015, Suzlon completed the sale of Senvion - the renamed REpower, the crown jewel of the 2007 buying spree - to the American private equity firm Centerbridge. Hansen had already been sold in 2011. The global empire Tanti bought was sold back to pay for the Indian company he built.

Even that was not enough. The restructuring outlived its deadlines; India's shift to auction-based wind contracts squeezed margins; CARE cut Suzlon's rating to default in April 2019, with $172 million of convertible bonds coming due that July. Market value, once Rs 109 billion after the Shanghvi deal, touched Rs 33 billion in May 2019. Shanghvi, asked about his investment that year, conceded it had not had a great outcome (Business Standard, 2019). The white knight was under water too.

Tulsi Tanti died of cardiac arrest on Saturday, 1 October 2022. He was 64; the company informed the exchanges, and Forbes recorded that he was survived by his wife and his children, Nidhi and Pranav. The family still held about 15% of the company - nearly all of it pledged to lenders. What he left behind was 13.5 gigawatts of installed wind, roughly a third of India's total, and a company mid-surgery: a 2020 preferential allotment had brought in capital, and a Rs 1,200-crore rights issue in 2022 - subscribed in full by the promoters, the Tanti family putting its own money back in - had steadied the balance sheet. His brother Girish Tanti carried on as vice chairman, and carries the company still.

What followed is the rarest thing in Indian business: a completed turnaround. By the 2023-24 annual report, Suzlon was debt-free with a net cash surplus. FY26 revenue ran past $1.75 billion. The company that defaulted on $209 million in 2012 now holds a 6-gigawatt order book - 78% of it from state utilities and commercial-industrial customers - and is raising the share of higher-margin EPC work from 38% toward 50% by FY28. Its new DevCo business builds and owns wind assets itself - the full-stack model the founders call Suzlon 2.0. Chief executive Ajay Kapur expects India's annual wind market to grow from 8 gigawatts to 13 in the next couple of years, inside the country's 100-gigawatt wind ambition for 2030.

blocks.html: Which brings the story back to this week. A younger Suzlon, the 2007 Suzlon, would have held the 17% line and let the story do the talking. This Suzlon cut the guidance on a record quarter, took the 8% fall the next day, and left three brokers' buy calls intact. Girish Tanti framed the moment in the release: a full-stack Suzlon 2.0, building toward India's 100-gigawatt ambition. The founder's version of this company sold the future. The successor's version is pricing the present.
The first Suzlon was built on what might happen. The second is built on what has been paid for. This week's guidance cut - discipline on a record quarter - is the whole difference.

blocks.alt: Editorial illustration of wind turbines on Indian farmland at golden hour with a winding road
blocks.caption: About a third of India's installed wind base carries this company's name.

blocks.html: The second life of Suzlon is not finished - margins, execution and a 6-gigawatt promise will see to that. But the arc is already complete: the wind man bet the family property on a machine he could not keep running, lost the empire keeping it, and his brothers bought the company back one rights issue at a time.

26.title: The wind man's second life
26.fact: A Slow Burn long read, Saturday 31 October 2026. On Thursday, Suzlon Energy reported record quarterly deliveries and 26% revenue growth - and cut its margin guidance; on Friday the market took 8% off the stock. The company behind that split verdict is the most dramatic arc in Indian business: a Surat textile family that built the world's most valuable wind-turbine maker, lost it to leverage, sold the crown jewels, buried the founder, and came back debt-free.
26.intro: The story in one line: what carried Tulsi Tanti up - leverage and ambition - nearly killed his company; what brought it back - selling the jewels, a white knight, the family doubling down - was unglamorous. This week's guidance cut is the same discipline, applied early.

27.title: The proudest father in finance
27.fact: A Slow Burn long read, Sunday 1 November 2026. Tomorrow morning, EAAA India Alternatives - the alternative-investment platform Edelweiss built from nothing in 2008 - lists on the BSE and NSE at Rs 1,665 a share, a Rs 1,200-crore offer subscribed just over five times. It is the second business the group has incubated to a listing. The first, Nuvama, is now worth about 2.6 times its parent. This is how a house mortgaged for a licence became an incubator - and what three crises taught it.
27.intro: The story in one line: Rashesh Shah and Venkat Ramaswamy built a financial group the hard way - no conglomerate behind it, crisis after crisis - lost it once to a liquidity storm, and came back by learning to build businesses, grow them up, and let them go.

blocks.html: On Monday 2 November, EAAA India Alternatives lists on both exchanges at Rs 1,665 a share - the top of its band and its final price, with allotment completed on 29 October (CNBC-TV18's IPO tracker). The issue is Rs 1,200 crore, entirely an offer for sale by the Edelweiss group; not a rupee goes to the company. At this price the platform is valued at about Rs 10,765 crore (Mint's IPO primer). Demand was lopsided: institutions bid 13.13 times their quota while retail barely covered at 1.03 - 5.25 times overall on the exchange tally carried by CNBC-TV18, 5.51 on ET's count - a debut carried by professional money.

blocks.svg: EAAA India Alternatives IPO, times subscribed by quota, 26-28 Oct 2026; source: exchange data via CNBC-TV18

blocks.html: EAAA manages money in what it calls real assets - infrastructure, commercial real estate - and private credit, most of it special-situations lending to companies in circumstances too unusual for a bank. Fee-paying assets under management stand at Rs 48,623 crore, and 75-80% of the private-credit book is special situations (Mint's September interview with chairman Rashesh Shah and EAAA chief executive Amit Agarwal, read in full). It is the second child Edelweiss has raised to a listing. To understand why the parent is smaller than both its children - and why Shah says that makes him "the proudest father" - you have to start in 1995, with a mortgaged house.

blocks.alt: Editorial illustration of a white edelweiss flower growing from a cracked stone slab with geometric mountains behind
blocks.caption: The edelweiss: an alpine flower that grows on rock - a company name with no founder or family behind it (Forbes).

groups.heading: 2. A mortgaged house and a sold stock

blocks.html: Rashesh Shah was drawn to statistics as a student, skipped his family's stationery business for IIM Ahmedabad, and joined ICICI in 1989 - when it was not yet a bank. There he met Venkat Ramaswamy, who went on to manage money at Spartek, India's first foreign private equity fund. Shah left to head research and investments at Prime Securities; in late 1995 he made the call: "it was a good time to start our own business" (Forbes India's 2015 history, read in full - the source for this chapter's scenes).

The plan was a boutique investment bank at Nariman Point, which needed a Category I merchant-banking licence - Rs 1 crore of capital. Shah convinced his father to mortgage the family house at Mahalaxmi. Ramaswamy sold the Infosys shares he held from the company's pre-IPO days - a connection from his ICICI years with Narayana Murthy. They raised the crore. Then Sebi moved the bar to Rs 5 crore, and the IPO-advisory plan was dead on arrival. Shah calls what happened next the company's first lesson: unable to work on public issues, Edelweiss helped first-generation entrepreneurs raise private capital instead - a business the big firms ignored. "We believed in finding opportunity amidst adversity," the company's own history says (Edelweiss's official timeline).

The early years were thin. The two founders paid themselves Rs 25,000 a month for five years. Their first mandate - raising about Rs 30 crore for a south Indian auto-parts maker, Madras Suspensions - failed to close. "My gut feel," Ramaswamy told Forbes, "is that if we had closed the Madras Suspensions deal, Edelweiss would have been a different type of company." The first win came in 1999: the sale of Thiruvananthapuram-based Peninsula Polymers to Japan's Terumo. Then came Rediff, India Infoline, Daksh and Educomp as clients; an angel cheque of Rs 1 crore from Madrid-based NRI Harish Fabiani in 1999; and in 2000, $2 million from Connect Capital for a tenth of the company.

blocks.alt: Editorial illustration of a tiny sapling in a pot on an oversized 1990s office desk with a skyline of simple rectangles behind
blocks.caption: 1995: the licence money came from a mortgaged house and a sold block of Infosys shares - then the regulator moved the bar anyway.

blocks.html: Through the 2000s Edelweiss grew by adjacency: investment banking led to institutional broking (it bought Rooshnil Securities along the way), which led to the insight that the real profit pool was credit - "the profit pool in capital markets is about one-twentieth that of the pool in the credit business," Shah reasoned. Credit needed Rs 100 crore of net worth; Edelweiss had Rs 54 crore. London-based Greater Pacific Capital put in Rs 80 crore, buying out Connect Capital and adding fresh money, and in 2006 Edelweiss formed its NBFC, ECL Finance. Lehman Brothers took 26% of ECL; after Lehman's own collapse in 2008, Edelweiss bought the stake back. The company listed in 2007, codified a "10x10" strategy - ten-fold in ten years - and by 2008-09 began assembling the retail platform: mortgages, a life-insurance joint venture with Japan's Tokio Marine, a mutual fund.

The quiet masterpiece of those years was the asset reconstruction company. In 2008, a senior hire from Arcil - India's oldest ARC - came over to build Edelweiss's challenger, seeded with Rs 45 crore and three unglamorous assets: a denim unit in Ahmedabad, a poultry farm in Hyderabad, a milk-processing plant in Punjab. The thesis: buy distressed loans at deep discounts and nurse the companies back. By December 2014 the ARC managed Rs 18,500 crore across more than 450 companies - larger than Arcil itself. Also in 2008, the group incorporated a small subsidiary to run alternative-investment strategies for institutions and the wealthy. It named it Edelweiss Alternative Asset Advisors - the company that lists tomorrow.

groups.heading: 4. The discipline, and the licence that never came

blocks.html: Edelweiss's culture was risk-first, and for years it showed. When the Rs 5,690-crore NSEL crisis hit in 2013, Edelweiss had refused the brokerage fees others chased, because it could not control the collateral - "we prefer a situation where we manage the collateral and then fund it," Shah said. It kept 150 people in risk alone. FY14 closed with revenue of Rs 2,556 crore and profit of Rs 220 crore, compounding above 35% for three years. But the big prize eluded it: in 2013 the RBI invited applications for new bank licences, and Edelweiss - built, in one rival CEO's admiring phrase, like "Goldman Sachs" flanked around capital markets - did not get one. Shah was philosophical: "We are hungry but we are not bhookad [ravenous]." He aimed to grow credit 30% a year to 2019-20. The machine he built to do it was about to meet its storm.

In September 2018, IL&FS - an infrastructure financier banks had treated as safe - defaulted, and the market suddenly asked who else was borrowing short to lend long (The Hindu, September 2018). The answer sold first and checked later: DHFL fell almost 60% intraday before closing 42% down (The Hindu, that day); on 8 October, Edelweiss Financial cracked 13% (Business Standard, that day). Edelweiss had no IL&FS-style hole, but it had Rs 50,000 crore of borrowings and a wholesale book, and for an NBFC in a liquidity panic, structure is guilt. "We have been grappling with liquidity over the last 18 months," Shah conceded in July 2020 (Mint, July 2020, read in full).

The reckoning was honest and it was brutal. Edelweiss cut borrowings from Rs 50,000 crore to Rs 33,000 crore in a year, shrank the wholesale loan book 43% to Rs 10,000 crore, and in March 2020 reported a quarterly loss of Rs 2,245 crore - its first loss in 25 years - after making Rs 2,549 crore of provisions. Then it amputated: ECL Finance would exit wholesale lending entirely by 2022, taking the credit risk into funds, where investors - not the balance sheet - hold it. The company that wanted to be a bank chose to become something else: an asset manager of other people's risk.

blocks.alt: Editorial illustration of a white edelweiss flower bent in a dark storm with petals tearing loose
blocks.caption: 2018-20: a liquidity panic, Rs 2,549 crore of provisions, and the first loss in 25 years.

blocks.html: The rebuild had a price: the children. In 2021, Singapore-based alternative investor PAG bought a majority of Edelweiss Wealth Management - the crown-jewel broking-and-wealth franchise built over two decades. On 26 September 2023, that business listed as Nuvama Wealth Management, with PAG holding about 56%; Edelweiss shareholders received 30% of the company in the demerger (Nuvama's listing release). This September, Nuvama carried a market value of about Rs 33,448 crore - about 2.6 times its parent's Rs 12,873 crore. Shah's verdict on being outgrown by his own creation is the title of this story: "If my kids do better than I do, I will be the proudest father" (Mint, September 2026).

Edelweiss stopped trying to own the whole orchard. It became a nursery: build businesses from seed, bring in partners when they need capital, list them when they can stand, and let the parent's value ride on the children.

The model has kept compounding. In January 2026, Carlyle agreed to buy the group's housing-finance arm, Nido Home Finance, for Rs 2,100 crore. Seven businesses remain under the listed parent - alternatives, asset management, the ARC, an NBFC, a mortgage lender, and two insurers. EAAA, Shah says, was built "from ground up, no foreign partnership." Alternatives as a share of India's GDP was 3.6% in 2024 and is expected to reach 4.16% by 2030, according to EAAA's own prospectus - the wind at the child's back.

An honest history has to include the bruises. On 29 May 2024, the Reserve Bank of India barred ECL Finance from structured transactions on its wholesale exposures and barred Edelweiss's ARC from acquiring fresh financial assets, citing evergreening concerns (Reuters, May 2024) - the regulator's way of saying the group had made stressed loans look healthier than they were. The group engaged, remediated, and on 17 December 2024 the RBI lifted both sets of restrictions, satisfied with the measures put in place (RBI's own press release, read in full). In September 2025, Sebi closed adjudication proceedings against Edelweiss's stressed-assets fund trust and the EAAA investment manager through a settlement order, after investor complaints on its SCORES platform (the Sebi order). And tomorrow's listing is itself the second attempt: the first draft prospectus, filed in December 2024 for Rs 1,500 crore (NDTV Profit), was returned by Sebi - Business Standard reported resubmission plans in April 2025 (Business Standard) - and the company came back with an issue Rs 300 crore smaller (Mint). The lesson the group took from 2018 holds: survive first, grow second.

The listing is a verdict on the incubator doctrine. EAAA arrives with Rs 48,623 crore of fee-paying assets, a special-situations franchise its CEO calls "the harder capability to build," institutional demand thirteen times over - and retail demand that barely covered. It is an offer for sale, so Edelweiss the parent, not EAAA, receives the proceeds; the child gets a public currency and a price that must now answer to a quarterly market. Watch three things from here: whether the stock holds the Rs 1,665 print; whether the parent - still carrying the memory of 2018 and the restraint it taught - re-rates as more children are listed or sold; and whether retail money, so hesitant in the book-building, arrives after the bell.

Thirty years of Edelweiss reduce to one inversion: the founders mortgaged a house to start it; the group now sells houses to grow. What carried it through was the oldest rule on Dalal Street - survive first.

blocks.alt: Editorial illustration of a shorter mature tree standing beside two taller young trees at sunrise
blocks.caption: Nuvama is worth about 2.6 times its parent. On Monday, the markets price the second child.

blocks.html: Sources read in full for this story: Forbes India's 2015 company history; Edelweiss's own timeline; Mint's 2020 wholesale-exit report and its September 2026 Shah-Agarwal interview; the Hindu and Business Standard's September-October 2018 crisis coverage; the RBI's May 2024 action and December 2024 lifting (both primary releases); Sebi's September 2025 settlement order page; Nuvama's 2023 listing release; NDTV Profit and Business Standard on the first DRHP; Mint and CNBC-TV18 on the IPO's terms and subscription. Prices are the IPO's stated terms; Monday's open is its own truth.

To understand why CDSL exists, picture Indian share ownership in the early 1990s: a physical certificate, a transfer deed, a signature match at the company's registrar, and weeks of waiting - with the ever-present risk that the paper was forged, stolen or simply "bad delivery," the market's term for a certificate that would not transfer cleanly. The 1992 securities scandal showed how easily paper could be printed into existence. Parliament's answer was dematerialisation: shares as entries in a central electronic vault. The first vault went to the establishment - the National Securities Depository, promoted by the country's largest institutions. The Bombay Stock Exchange, suddenly facing a rival-owned pipe under its own market, promoted a second: Central Depository Services (India) Ltd, incorporated in Mumbai on 12 December 1997 (CDSL's offer document, on Sebi's site), opening for business in 1999 (CDSL's investor presentation, read in full).

The division of spoils looked settled before it began. The older depository, owned by the country's biggest financial institutions, took the institutions: the custodial accounts, the foreign funds, the blue-chip registers. CDSL got what was left - the retail edge of the market, the small broker, the small investor. It is the oldest pattern in infrastructure: one player is handed the present; the other is left the future, if it can survive long enough to collect.

blocks.alt: Editorial illustration of torn paper certificates dissolving into an ordered stream of small squares
blocks.caption: Dematerialisation: a mountain of paper certificates becoming a single ordered stream of entries.

blocks.html: Survival took patience. CDSL crossed one million demat accounts only in 2005 - six years in, a rounding error next to the incumbent's institutional book. What it did with the wait matters more than the wait: it built for the customer nobody else was courting. It pioneered e-voting for shareholders in 2009, turning corporate governance from a postal ritual into a click; by the end of January 2012 it had ten thousand issuers admitting their securities - equities, bonds, debentures, commercial paper, mutual fund units - into its system; it built e-DIS, replacing the physical delivery-instruction slip with a digital mandate. Each product was small. Each one assumed the account holder was a person, not an institution (all milestones from the company's own investor presentation).

groups.heading: 3. The listing that made it real

blocks.html: In June 2017, twenty years after incorporation, BSE brought its depository to market - and CDSL became India's, and Asia-Pacific's, first listed depository (company timeline). The market's verdict was immediate: the stock listed at a 68% premium to its issue price on 30 June 2017 (Business Line, that day). A utility - the plumbing - had become a stock people wanted to own, because by 2017 the plumbing was the growth story: every new investor India added had to pass through a depository, and increasingly that depository was CDSL.

blocks.alt: Editorial illustration of a shorter tower overtaking a taller one as squares flow upward through it
blocks.caption: 2019: the challenger passes the incumbent in accounts - and has not looked back.

blocks.html: In 2019 CDSL became India's largest depository by number of demat accounts, a position it has held since (investor presentation). Then came the flood. The pandemic year turned the smartphone into a broker's office, and the discount brokers India's new investors signed up with ran their plumbing through CDSL. In 2023 it crossed 100 million demat accounts - the first depository in the country to do so - having taken six years for its first million and then adding them by the crore. It rolled with the market's biggest structural upgrades: T+1 settlement and pledge instructions in 2022, mandatory direct payout of securities to investor accounts in 2025, twenty-five years of operations marked in 2024. By FY24 it held 76% market share with 11.56 crore investor accounts (company annual report). The gap in accounts is now a chasm: 18.01 crore BO accounts at 31 March 2026 on CDSL's own Q4FY26 deck, against the older depository's 3.95 crore in the comparison drawn ahead of NSDL's own listing (NDTV Profit) - which finally arrived on 6 August 2025, eight years after the challenger showed the way (Economic Times).

Saturday's numbers show the machine at work. CDSL's September-quarter net profit rose 24% to Rs 174 crore against Rs 140 crore a year ago; revenue rose to Rs 394 crore from Rs 319 crore; about 75 lakh new demat accounts opened in the quarter alone; assets under custody crossed Rs 89 lakh crore; the account base grew about 17% year on year (Business Line, read in full). "Despite global macroeconomic volatility, participation in securities market continues to demonstrate resilience," said Nehal Vora, the managing director and chief executive - a market-plumbing lifer who was BSE's chief regulatory officer before Sebi cleared his appointment to CDSL's top job in 2019. The economics are the kind analysts dream about: once the vault is built, every additional account, transaction and issuer costs almost nothing to serve - a business where growth falls mostly to the bottom line.

But keep two honest caveats on the record. First, the machine tracks the market's mood: through FY26, as the correction bit, CDSL's standalone quarterly operating income slipped from Rs 221 crore to Rs 212 crore and net profit from Rs 152 crore to Rs 90 crore (company presentation) - before the FY27 rebound that Saturday's print confirms. Second, the machine has failed in public: in April 2025, Sebi made CDSL deposit Rs 3 crore as a financial disincentive for technical glitches (CDSL's own exchange intimation) - the regulator's way of saying that when the pipes burst, the whole market waits. A depository that is most of the country's accounts is also most of the country's single point of failure.

blocks.alt: Editorial illustration of a precise machine of gears balancing on a thin fulcrum
blocks.caption: Annuity economics on a fulcrum: growth falls to the bottom line - until the machine itself stumbles.

blocks.html: Which sets up the decision in front of Vora now. The account-opening flood that built CDSL cannot run forever: 18 crore accounts is already a large fraction of India's plausible investing population, the regulator watches fees on market plumbing with a hawk's patience, and from August 2025 the older depository is listed too - with its own shareholders to answer and an incentive to fight for the retail account it once ignored. CDSL's answer, visible in its own disclosures, is to carry its franchise beyond the equity vault: an investment in India International Bullion Holding IFSC - the GIFT City bullion exchange's holding company - to support its technology; a strategic stake in ONDC, the open commerce network; an insurance-repository subsidiary signing software partnerships beyond its original brief (Business Line). None of these is yet a business on the scale of the vault. Together they are an admission: the flood was a gift, and the next twenty years have to be built.

The paper rot made CDSL necessary; retail India made it big; the listing made it rich. What makes it last is the question its own chief executive is now paid to answer - and the honest way to read Saturday's 24% jump is not as proof of permanence, but as one more quarter of running room in which to find out.

Sources read for this long read: CDSL's investor presentation and annual reports (company site), the 2017 offer document (Sebi's site), Business Line's listing-day and Q2 reports, the company's intimation of the Sebi disincentive, NDTV Profit's depository comparison, and the Economic Times on NSDL's listing. Every figure is from those documents; nothing here is investment advice.

28.title: The pipes under the market
28.fact: A Slow Burn long read, Monday 2 November 2026. Every share an Indian investor owns sits in one of two vaults. The smaller, younger one - Central Depository Services, CDSL - opened for business in 1999 with almost nothing, became the first listed depository in Asia, and now holds the accounts of most of the country's investors - 18 crore of them. On Saturday it posted a 24% profit jump, with 75 lakh new demat accounts opened in a single quarter. This is how India's market forgot paper - and what the company that made it happen is worth worrying about next.

hero.alt: Editorial illustration of an abstract network of pipelines carrying glowing paper slips into a central hub
hero.caption: Every trade in India ends in one of two depositories. The younger one now carries most of the country's investors.

groups.heading: 1. The rot that made a monopoly

blocks.html: Before Coal India, Indian coal was hundreds of small private mines and a national embarrassment. The seams were rich; the industry was not. Private owners under-invested, practised what the official record calls "slaughter mining" - extracting the easiest coal and wasting the rest - and kept their workers in conditions the government's own historians describe as sub-standard. The 1970s oil shock forced the question: a Fuel Policy Committee concluded that coal, not imported crude, had to be India's primary source of commercial energy, and coal could not carry that weight while it stayed fragmented and starved of capital (Coal India's own history, read in full).

The man who designed the fix was Mohan Kumaramangalam, the steel-and-mines minister who argued that only nationalisation could deliver what the industry needed: conservation of scarce coking coal, planned development, safety standards, investment at scale, and a decent life for the workforce. It happened in two stages. On 16 October 1971 the government promulgated the Coking Coal Mines (Emergency Provisions) Act, and on 1 May 1972 it nationalised 226 coking-coal mines, folding them into a new company, Bharat Coking Coal. On 31 January 1973 an ordinance took over the management of 711 non-coking mines; they were nationalised from 1 May 1973 under a new Coal Mines Authority. Then, in November 1975, the state formed a formal holding company over both - Coal India Limited. The company his design produced would become the largest coal miner on Earth.

blocks.alt: Flat geometric illustration of an oversized order book overflowing with bid slips
blocks.caption: Bids worth Rs 2.35 lakh crore chased a Rs 15,400 crore issue - a demand record that stood for years.

blocks.html: For thirty-five years the monopoly dug coal quietly, and then the government needed money. In October 2010 it put 10% of Coal India up for sale - an offer of 63.1 crore shares in a Rs 225-245 band, aiming to raise up to Rs 15,400 crore, the largest public issue India had ever attempted, beating Reliance Power's Rs 11,700 crore from 2008. The market's answer was staggering: bids worth Rs 2,34,716 crore - the most demand any primary market in the country's history had generated, surpassing even Reliance Power's frenzied 2008 book; the institutional slice alone was covered 24.7 times, and foreign investors bid Rs 1.20 lakh crore, more than they had put into all Indian stocks that entire year (PTI's record-day report, read in full). "Every record is meant to be broken by someone. CIL issue is a blockbuster," said V Jaya Sankar of Kotak Investment Banking, one of six book-runners.

The listing was timed, deliberately or not, like a festival gift. On 4 November 2010 - the day before Diwali - Coal India opened for trading and surged as much as 40.7% above the issue price, closing its first day with a market value of $48.9 billion: instantly India's fourth-largest listed company, ahead of nearly every bank and software giant on the boards (Reuters, from that day). A 35-year-old state monopoly had become the stock market's newest blue chip in a single morning. Yet the same day's report carried the seed of every later problem: even as investors celebrated, the company was making non-binding bids for coal projects in Australia and Indonesia - because India, sitting on some of the world's largest reserves, already could not dig enough to feed itself.

The number that has haunted Coal India for a decade is one billion tonnes. Successive governments set it as the production target that would end coal imports; successive Coal Indias missed it. The formal public commitment came on the company's 45th foundation day in November 2019, when coal minister Pralhad Joshi announced Coal India would produce one billion tonnes by 2024 (the government's own press release). Reality was already behind schedule: in the year that announcement landed, Coal India produced 602 million tonnes and missed its own annual target (Business Standard, April 2020). The 2024 deadline passed unmet. The target now sits at 2030.

And while the company chased the number, the ground under its monopoly was cut away. On 18 June 2020, Prime Minister Modi launched the auction of 41 coal blocks for commercial mining - private companies, for the first time since 1973, allowed to dig coal and sell it in the open market, no end-use conditions attached; the blocks on offer alone held annual production capacity of nearly a third of national output (Reuters, June 2020). The reform Kumaramangalam's nationalisation had made unthinkable - private coal, sold commercially - became policy forty-seven years later, not because the state company failed, but because India kept importing coal while its monopoly could not grow fast enough. Coal India kept its reserves, its scale and its customers. It lost the wall around them.

groups.heading: 4. The machine today: strong quarter, honest cracks

blocks.alt: Flat geometric illustration of two diverging lines, one rising gently, one dipping
blocks.caption: Production fell about 2.5% in the first half while offtake rose 7.6% - the gap was filled by emptying the stockyard.

blocks.html: Thursday's results show the machine at its most profitable. For July-September, Coal India's consolidated profit after tax rose 57% year-on-year to Rs 6,547 crore - or, measured as profit attributable to the company's owners, up 53% to Rs 6,516 crore; both figures come straight from its exchange filing and both are correct on their own basis. Revenue rose 21% to Rs 44,179 crore, EBITDA rose 28% to Rs 11,447 crore as margins widened to 26%, and the board declared a second interim dividend of Rs 10.25 a share - the record date is tomorrow, with payment by 27 November (the results, read against the filing). The driver was better realisations: the same coal, sold dearer.

The cracks are in the ground, not the accounts. In the first half of this financial year, Coal India produced 321 million tonnes - down from 329 a year earlier - while offtake, the coal actually shipped to customers, rose 7.6% to 384 million tonnes. A company cannot ship more than it digs forever; the gap was filled by emptying the stockyard, drawing inventories down by 63.7 million tonnes, from 130 million tonnes in April to 66.6 by September. Sequentially, profit fell 26% from the June quarter's Rs 8,850 crore. The quarter's headline, in other words, is a realisation story laid over a production problem - the same production problem the billion-tonne target has been missing for a decade.

groups.heading: 5. The reform year, and the man betting on the next two decades

blocks.html: The man now carrying that problem is B Sairam, Coal India's chairman and managing director, a company lifer who took over the top job and promptly declared 2026 a "year of reform and transformation": mechanised loading for exact quantity and quality, digitised mines, faster rail evacuation, and safety upgrades - "the twin priorities are increased output and improved supplies of quality coal," he told PTI (ET's interview). In August he put a number on the ambition: a Rs 1 trillion investment programme in coal evacuation and gasification, aimed at reaching the one-billion-tonne mark by FY30 - the third deadline the target has worn - while ruling out an immediate coal price hike despite rising costs (Mint's report, read in full).

Sairam's deeper bet is strategic, and he states it without flinching: coal will stay "at the top of the energy mix" for India's near and medium term, and, with the bulk of generation to be met by coal for at least the next two decades, central to it for just as long. The case for the bet is arithmetic - India still burns coal for most of its electricity, and demand keeps growing with every data centre and air conditioner. The case against is direction - every rupee of the trillion goes into the durability of the fuel the world is leaving, while private miners, freed in 2020, attack the same customers without the pension baggage. It is the classic incumbent's wager, made by a man who has spent his career inside the machine: that the transition will be slow enough, and Indian demand large enough, for the world's biggest coal company to keep winning the game it was nationalised to play.

blocks.alt: Flat geometric illustration of a single dark monolith surrounded by rising solar-panel shapes
blocks.caption: The incumbent's wager: a trillion rupees that India's energy transition will be slow enough.

groups.heading: 6. What sixteen years settled, and what they did not

blocks.html: Stand at tomorrow's record date and look back at Diwali eve 2010. The IPO's promise was that market discipline would modernise the monopoly: capital, scrutiny, accountability. Sixteen years on, the record is genuinely mixed. The company that listed that day has paid its owners rivers of dividends, kept the lights on through every demand shock, and just posted a 57% profit jump. It has also missed its own production century three times running, watched its monopoly be legislated away, and answered its output problem by draining the stockyard. What sixteen years settled: the market can own a monopoly and be paid handsomely for it. What they did not: whether a trillion-rupee bet on coal's durability is the company's renewal or its most expensive act of nostalgia. B Sairam gets to answer that one - and unlike his target, his deadline is not his to choose.

Sources read for this long read: Coal India’s own corporate history; PTI’s and Reuters’ coverage of the 2010 IPO and listing; the coal ministry’s 2019 press release on the billion-tonne target; Business Standard on the FY20 miss; Reuters on the 2020 commercial-mining auctions; PTI and Mint interviews with CMD B Sairam; and Coal India’s Q2 FY27 results as filed with the exchanges, read via moneycontrol’s full report. 30.title: The oil merchant's brands
30.fact: A Slow Burn long read, Wednesday 4 November 2026. On Tuesday, Marico reported its strongest volume quarter in years and the stock rose 9.4%. Behind that number is a thirty-five-year build: a third-generation commodity trader who looked at fifteen-kilo tins of coconut oil and saw a consumer brand, carved a company out of his family's business in 1990, took it public in 1996, bought brands off global giants, and survived the bets that did not work. This is how Parachute and Saffola became national defaults - and what the latest quarter says the machine is still doing right.

hero.alt: Flat geometric editorial illustration of oil tins transforming into repeating branded bottle shapes
hero.caption: From fifteen-kilo commodity tins to branded bottles on a national shelf - the Marico transformation in one image.

segments.label: What the story leaves you with

blocks.html: Harsh Mariwala did not found a startup; he inherited a trading desk. His grandfather and father had incorporated Bombay Oil Industries, a family firm that traded the oils an old Bombay merchant house traded - coconut, groundnut, safflower - sold in bulk, in fifteen-kilo tin cans, to intermediaries who owned the customer relationship (Mariwala's own first-person account in Harvard Business Review). Fresh out of Sydenham College in 1971, he joined the family business and found the commodity trader's classic trap: real volume, no pricing power, and a product whose maker the end consumer never knew (Harvard Business School's oral history).

The insight that built everything came from looking at the tin. Oils sold loose and anonymous could be sold branded and packaged - Parachute coconut oil and Saffola refined oil already existed as small family brands inside the business, and the young Mariwala spent the 1970s and 1980s pushing them from tin cans into consumer packs, building distribution one town at a time in a country where coconut oil was bought on habit, not advertising. The company's own anniversary report marks the moment: the blue bottle's first appearance in the 1980s was, it says, Harsh's first innovation - traditional tin packs replaced by plastic, pioneering an industry-wide shift (Economic Times profile). The lesson he has repeated ever since: in a commodity business, the brand is not decoration - it is the entire margin.

blocks.alt: Flat geometric illustration of a small office block separating from a large warehouse
blocks.caption: In 1990 the branded business stepped out of the family commodity house - a new company, a new identity, and by 1992 its own office.

blocks.html: By the late 1980s the branded business had outgrown its home inside a trading firm. The corporate shell was incorporated in 1988; the branded consumer business itself was created in 1990 as an offshoot of Bombay Oil Industries - deliberately separate, with its own professional managers and its own culture. The company's own anniversary timeline starts the story on 2 April 1990 and records the first overseas office, in Dubai, in 1992-94 - Parachute reaching the Gulf's Indian diaspora before most Indian consumer companies had looked outward at all (Marico's 25-year anniversary report, read in full; INSEAD's case study).

The separation was the making of the firm. Inside a commodities house, a brand is one line among many; inside its own company, it is the whole reason to exist. The breakaway let Marico hire differently - professional managers rather than family traders - and price risk differently: a bad quarter in copra could hurt, but it could no longer sink an unrelated trading book, and a great brand idea no longer had to compete for capital with a commodity position.

In 1996 Marico listed on the Indian stock exchange in an IPO-cum-offer-for-sale - the step that turned a family offshoot into a listed company. The company's own arithmetic on what followed: a rupee invested at the IPO was worth Rs 117 by March 2016, a 27% compounded annual return, nearly eighteen times the Sensex over the same twenty years (the anniversary report). What the listing financed was an acquisition habit that became Marico's second engine: buying under-loved brands and running them harder than their owners had. In 2006 it bought Nihar, a coconut-oil brand, from Hindustan Unilever - the boldest version of the play, taking a rival's asset and folding it into the Parachute system. In 2012 it bought Set Wet, Livon and Zatak - the erstwhile Paras Pharmaceuticals personal-care brands - from Reckitt Benckiser, agreements signed that February and completed that May, extending from oils into male grooming and hair care (Marico's own results release).

The honest ledger includes the misses. The most visible experiment was Kaya, a chain of skin-care clinics launched in the 2000s - a services business inside a products company, later separated into its own entity after years of dragging on the core. The pattern matters more than any single deal: Marico kept testing adjacencies, kept what compounded, and cut what did not. A consumer company that never misses is not taking enough swings; the discipline is in the cutting.

blocks.alt: Flat geometric illustration of rising volume bars beside a falling cost curve
blocks.caption: Copra costs fell; Marico passed some of it through as sharper pricing, and volumes answered with their best quarter in 22 quarters.

blocks.html: Tuesday's quarter showed the old machine still learning. Consolidated profit rose 31% for July-September, ahead of estimates, helped by cheaper copra - the coconut kernel that is Parachute's core input - and the company raised its growth guidance for the year (Moneycontrol's report). The number inside the number: Parachute's volumes grew 13%, the strongest in 22 quarters, taking volume market share above 60%, per the company's information update reported by Hindu BusinessLine - meaning the input-cost windfall was partly passed to consumers as sharper pricing rather than banked entirely as margin. The stock rose 9.44% on the BSE to Rs 873.20, its high of the day, leading the FMCG pack that carried the whole market to a two-month high.

Read against the founder's original insight, the quarter is a late proof. A commodity input fell in price; a trader would have banked the spread; a brand-builder bought volume and share with it instead. Fifty-five years after a Sydenham graduate walked into his family's oil business, that is still the whole strategy in one decision.

groups.heading: 5. What the story leaves you with

blocks.alt: Flat geometric illustration of a single bottle casting a long shadow shaped like a rising graph
blocks.caption: The brand is the margin: one decision, compounded for three decades.

blocks.html: Three transferable lessons, none of them new and all of them rare in practice. First, the escape from commodity economics runs through the consumer's memory, not the factory gate - packaging, distribution and trust are the product. Second, separation is strategy: the branded business only compounded once it had its own company, its own people and its own P&L. Third, acquisitions are a skill built in reps - Marico's hits worked because the misses were survived, sized and cut. The next test for the machine is already visible: input costs cycle back up, and the same choice - bank the margin or buy the volume - arrives in reverse. The company's own history says which way it usually answers.
