31.title: The exchange under the banyan tree
31.fact: A Slow Burn long read, Thursday 5 November 2026. On Wednesday evening, BSE Ltd reported a 45% jump in quarterly profit - hours after its stock had fallen 1.75% ahead of the print. Behind that shrug is the strangest comeback in Indian finance: a 150-year-old exchange founded under a banyan tree, nearly written off after a younger rival took its business, then revived in three years by a chief executive who rebuilt its derivatives market from almost nothing to a quarter of the country's volume. This is how the Bombay Stock Exchange died, and came back.

hero.alt: Flat geometric editorial illustration of a banyan tree whose canopy morphs into the tower of an old stock exchange
hero.caption: From a banyan tree near Bombay's Town Hall to the 29-storey Phiroze Jeejeebhoy Towers - one institution, 150 years.

blocks.html: The Bombay Stock Exchange began with a membership fee of one rupee. On 9 July 1875, a few dozen brokers who had been trading under a banyan tree near the Town Hall in South Bombay resolved to form an association - the Native Share and Stock Brokers' Association - each contributing Re 1 (NDTV Profit's 150th-anniversary account). The man behind it was Premchand Roychand, the cotton king of Bombay, then one of the richest merchants in the city. The association was formally constituted by indenture on 3 December 1887, making it the oldest stock exchange in Asia (the exchange's own company history, drawn from its listing prospectus).

The early survival story is worth keeping because it is a credit story. The brokers settled into a trading hall on Dalal Street and struggled to pay the rent; Dinshaw Maneckji Petit - founder of one of India's first textile mills - bailed them out by donating shares in his Victoria Manufacturing Co., which the brokers sold, repaid, and built on; by 1899 they had their own building, named for him. On 31 August 1957, the exchange became the first in the country to win permanent recognition under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act (NDTV Profit; company history). By its 150th anniversary in July 2025, the market value of the companies listed on it stood above Rs 462 lakh crore across 5,671 listings - and the address is still Dalal Street, now a 29-storey tower.

groups.heading: 2. The index, the machine - and the long slide

blocks.alt: Flat geometric illustration of nineteenth-century brokers exchanging paper slips under a tree, an oversized one-rupee coin in the foreground
blocks.caption: Re 1 each: the membership fee that founded Asia's oldest exchange in 1875.

blocks.html: Twice in its modern history the BSE built the thing the whole country would use. On 2 January 1986 it launched the Sensex - India's first equity index, base value 100 - the number that still defines "the market" in everyday speech; the index turned 40 this January (BSE's own milestones record). In 1995 it started BOLT, the Bombay Online Trading system, replacing the open-outcry pit with screens (company history). In 2000 came SEBI's approval to trade derivatives.

Then came the slide. A younger rival - the National Stock Exchange - took the cash business and then the derivatives business so completely that by this decade the BSE's share of India's daily cash-equity volume was just 7 to 8 percent, and the NSE had become the world's largest derivatives exchange (Business Standard's revival account, reported with Bloomberg). How dependent the BSE's derivatives business had become on paying for flow shows in its own IPO document: when the exchange withdrew its liquidity-incentive schemes in April 2016, equity-derivatives volume collapsed 99.9% - from over 20.8 lakh contracts a day in FY2015 to 1,446 a day in the six months to September 2016 (Moneycontrol's pre-IPO brief, from the prospectus). The oldest exchange in Asia was, in the business that mattered most, close to a shell.

The rescue began as paperwork. Under SEBI's corporatisation and demutualisation scheme of 20 May 2005, the member-owned club became a company - incorporated as Bombay Stock Exchange Limited on 8 August 2005, with ownership separated from trading rights; the scheme's appointed date followed on 16 May 2007. That same year Singapore Exchange and Deutsche Börse each bought 5% for about Rs 200.8 crore apiece. In 2011 it renamed itself BSE Limited (company history).

The public-market test came a decade later. On 23 January 2017 the BSE opened the first IPO by an Indian stock exchange - Rs 1,243 crore, priced at Rs 805-806, entirely an offer for sale by existing shareholders, with anchors including Goldman Sachs's asset-management arm and the Kuwait Investment Authority. The issue was subscribed 51 times (Economic Times), and on 3 February 2017 the BSE became India's first listed stock exchange - listed, by SEBI's no-self-listing rule, on the NSE (Moneycontrol; milestones). On 9 January, the Prime Minister had inaugurated its international arm, India INX, at GIFT City. The exchange that nearly missed its own industry's future had, at least, become investable in it.

blocks.alt: Flat geometric illustration of an old trading terminal on one side and a modern exchange tower on the other, with a falling-then-rising graph line
blocks.caption: From 1,446 derivatives contracts a day in 2016 to a 24% national share by end-2024 - the revival arc.

blocks.html: When Sundararaman Ramamurthy took charge as CEO in January 2023, few expected him to revitalise Asia's oldest exchange. In the two years that followed, the market value of the 150-year-old company rose nine-fold, revenues nearly tripled, and the dormant derivatives segment went from near-zero to 24% of national volume by December 2024 (Business Standard/Bloomberg). The method was unglamorous: weekly options contracts, smaller tick sizes in cash trading, and - tellingly - an end to the broker incentives whose withdrawal had collapsed the business in 2016.

The twist in the tale is personnel. Ramamurthy's predecessor, Ashish Kumar Chauhan, had built much of the BSE's modern technology stack - and then left to run the NSE, the rival he had spent years fighting. Ramamurthy inherited both the machine and the rivalry. His remaining problem is the cash market, where the BSE still holds only 7-8% of an $11-billion-a-day business; his fixes are plumbing - a single contract note across both exchanges, and a best-price rule whose own back-test suggested volumes could be 25-45% higher. The risks are equally concrete: SEBI's October 2024 curbs on options trading could shrink turnover by as much as 35%, and colocation - servers next to the exchange's own - already drives 65% of its derivatives volume, a concentrated and sophisticated clientele. His line, in the January 2025 interview: "We will leave no stone unturned."

groups.heading: 5. The quarter, and the next test

blocks.alt: Flat geometric illustration of a timeline from a small sapling to a tall illuminated tower under a rising graph line
blocks.caption: One hundred and fifty years in: the institution is the product, and the product is being rebuilt.

blocks.html: Which brings us to Wednesday. For July-September, BSE Ltd reported consolidated profit of Rs 809.15 crore, up 44.9% on the year, on revenue up 34.1% at Rs 1,432.6 crore; EBITDA rose 42.4% to Rs 984 crore at a 68.7% margin, and transaction charges - the fee line that rides trading volume - grew 42% to Rs 1,127.8 crore (Economic Times). The stock had fallen 1.75% through the session, ahead of the print - after a nine-fold run, a 45% profit quarter is simply what the price already assumes. That is what a fully re-rated revival looks like; the verdict on the gap lands Thursday.

The next test is already on the calendar, and it is the same one the January 2025 interview named: whether the derivatives revival survives a regulator determined to cool options speculation, and whether the cash-market push can dent a rival that is itself now listed - the NSE debuted on the BSE's own boards this September, which, as Ramamurthy noted with some pleasure, should itself send the BSE volume, since an exchange cannot list on itself. A hundred and fifty years after a rupee each under a banyan tree, Asia's oldest exchange is once again being run like a company with something to prove. Its founder-brokers, who could not make the rent until a mill owner paid it in shares, would recognise the condition.

32.title: The machine that weighed the gold
32.fact: A Slow Burn long read, Friday 6 November 2026. On Thursday, Titan Company reported quarterly profit up 114% to Rs 2,393 crore - a one-off customs-duty gain flattered the print, but the underlying business grew 18% - on the eve of the Diwali weekend its jewellery brand was built for. Behind that quarter is the least likely success in the Tata stable: a watch company that wandered into jewellery for export, nearly sank selling 18-karat Western designs to a country that buys 22-karat wedding gold, and was saved by an X-ray machine that proved India's jewellers were short-changing their customers. This is how Tanishq was built.

hero.alt: Flat geometric editorial illustration of a gold bangle passing through a scanning machine, with a watch face in the background
hero.caption: A watch company, a purity machine, and the trust machine it became: Titan’s jewellery business turned on one test.

blocks.html: Titan exists because of a phone call in March 1977. Xerxes Desai, then running Tata Press, got a call from his associate Anil Manchanda, who had been scouting new businesses for the group: “There are five projects I have shortlisted. The best among them is watches” (Tata’s own 40-year history). The market logic was blunt. In the 1970s, Indian buyers queued on waiting lists for sturdy mechanical watches from two domestic incumbents; the industry made about 1.5 million watches a year against a market worth at least 30 million, and smuggled foreign watches filled the gap (Tata’s heritage account).

The obstacles were the Licence Raj itself. The Swiss would not share movement technology; the government had reserved watchmaking for the public and small-scale sectors and denied the Tatas permission. The way in came through Iravatham Mahadevan, whom Desai had helped years earlier and who by 1979 ran TIDCO - the Tamil Nadu Industrial Development Corporation. TIDCO was talking to the French movement maker France Ebauches and needed a joint-venture partner. When Francois Perret of France Ebauches came to Bombay House to close the deal, JRD Tata - fluent in French - conducted the final negotiations himself, and when the fee seemed too high, traded acceptance of the price for more intensive training of the workforce (Tata’s heritage account). The name is an acronym: TI for Tata Industries, TAN for Tamil Nadu.

Titan Watches was incorporated in July 1984 - more than seven years after the project began, a stretch Desai said brought the team close to “abandoning the effort” more than once. Hosur, a small town in Tamil Nadu, became the factory site; Charles Correa designed the township; JRD dedicated the complex in March 1988. Quartz technology, sharp design and honest pricing made the watches bestsellers from the first ad - customers arrived at stores carrying newspaper cuttings. By its first year of operations, 1987-88, Titan was India’s leading producer of quartz analogue watches (Tata’s 40-year history).

groups.heading: 2. The detour that nearly sank the company

blocks.alt: Flat geometric illustration of a 1980s Indian watch factory with a French flag motif and quartz watch movements
blocks.caption: Hosur, 1984: France Ebauches movements, Charles Correa’s township, and quartz watches India queued for.

blocks.html: The jewellery business began as an export plant, and the reason was foreign exchange. Titan’s own imports were eating currency, and the government was encouraging exports; on a visit to a Mumbai jewellery exhibition in 1990, Desai and Titan’s PR head Jayanthi Prasad formed the idea. In mid-1993 Tata Sons approved the plan, and Titan built the finest jewellery plant it could in Hosur - an investment of Rs 65 crore, a huge sum then (C K Venkataraman’s account, excerpted on Rediff from his book The Tanishq Story).

It failed almost immediately. The plant, opened in 1994, was built for Western tastes - a small range of 18-karat, minimal-styled jewellery - without leaders who knew the export markets or buyers who wanted the product. “Of course, all this is in hindsight,” Venkataraman writes. With the investment stranded, Titan turned to the domestic market - and repeated the mistake at home. No consumer research was done on whether Indians would buy 18-karat jewellery; Desai was confident Titan would transform jewellery as it had watches. Tanishq - the name Desai built from Nishka, a throat ornament, swapping the k for a q and adding a ta in front - opened its first boutique on Cathedral Road, Chennai, in July 1996. It was modelled on European stores; customers were expected to make appointments; the staff were “like air hostesses.” First-year sales closed at Rs 2.8 crore against a target of Rs 3.5 crore, and the feedback was unambiguous: we need 22-karat (Rediff).

What Titan was up against was not taste but arithmetic. Indian jewellery was a store of value first: 22-karat gold (916 parts in 1,000), bought largely for weddings, made by hand by karigars, sold by family jewellers customers had trusted for generations. Ishaat Hussain, Tata Sons’ finance director and a Titan board member for over twenty years, could not see how the gaddi could be corporatized. Through the late 1990s the business bled, living off the watch division’s profits (NDTV Profit’s excerpt from Vinay Kamath’s TITAN: Inside India’s Most Successful Consumer Brand).

blocks.alt: Flat geometric illustration of an X-ray fluorescence machine analysing a gold ornament, a queue of customers behind
blocks.caption: The Karatmeter: three minutes, non-destructive, and devastating to an industry built on under-karatage.

blocks.html: The industry’s quiet secret was under-karatage. Because buyers resisted high making charges, many jewellers protected their margins by selling 19- or 20-karat gold as 22-karat; Titan’s own testing of jewellery from across the country had established this. The problem was proof: the standard test meant melting the piece. At the Basel jewellery and watch show in 1996, Titan’s manufacturing head M S Shantharam saw an X-ray fluorescence spectrometer - a machine that could read a metal alloy’s composition in three minutes without damaging it. Vasant Nangia, moved from London in 1997 to head jewellery, pushed the machines into boutiques nationwide at over Rs 10 lakh each, at a time when Tanishq’s finances could barely carry the bet. Titan’s team reprogrammed the devices for Indian alloys, working through forty-five to fifty gold standards. The Lintas agency named it the Karatmeter (Rediff).

The machine worked - as an indictment. Queues formed; customers wept or raged at discovering what their family jeweller had sold them; local jewellers leaned on Tanishq franchisees to stop using it, some with threats of violence. And sales still did not move. The breakthrough was a single customer encounter: a woman at the Dickenson Road store in Bangalore tested her jewellery, learned it was 17-karat, not 22, and snapped at then-COO Jacob Kurian, “You don’t do anything to solve our problem. All you do are things to make us feel bad.” The Karatmeter told people they had been cheated; Tanishq offered no remedy (NDTV Profit).

The remedy became the famous exchange scheme, branded 19=22: bring your old jewellery, test it on the Karatmeter, and if it read between 19 and 22 karat, Tanishq would exchange it for new 22-karat jewellery at full value - the customer paid only the making charges, and Tanishq bore the cost of the gold. The finance head nearly had a heart attack, Kurian recalled. The night it launched, a staffer called him from the store in excitement: “There are people in our store!” It was, he said, “like a zoo.” The scheme ran across India and converted the machine’s indictment into Tanishq’s founding promise (NDTV Profit).

blocks.alt: Flat geometric illustration of a modern Indian jewellery showroom at Diwali, lamps and gold necklaces
blocks.caption: Diwali weekend: the season Tanishq was rebuilt for, one purity test at a time.

blocks.html: The turnaround had a deadline. Kurian told his town halls the business had one year to turn around or they would all be out of jobs - the factory staff, paid the same wages as the profitable watch division, had no idea how badly Tanishq was doing. Harish Bhat, who had joined from Tata Tea in 2001 and took over as COO when Kurian left in 2003, recalls the Diwali festival sale that year: stores were dialled around the country at midnight to tally sales, and several crossed Rs 1 crore in a single day. The trust machine - transparent weights, purity on display, the exchange promise - had found its season (NDTV Profit).

What followed was compounding. Tanishq became India’s largest jewellery retailer; Titan layered on Zoya and Mia, eyewear (Titan EyePlus), and in 2016 paid Rs 357.24 crore for a 62% stake in CaratLane, the online jewellery startup - the omnichannel bet that aged well (Business Standard, from the BSE filing). For the full financial year 2025-26, Titan’s consolidated total income rose 33% to Rs 76,078 crore and profit rose 52% to Rs 5,073 crore (Business Today).

And then the quarter that pegs this story. On Thursday, Titan reported consolidated profit up 114% to Rs 2,393 crore for the September 2026 quarter - a figure inflated by a one-off gain from the change in gold customs duty, with adjusted pre-tax profit up 18% - on revenue of Rs 20,614 crore that missed street estimates (Hindu BusinessLine; Mint). The stock rose 1.72% on results eve. The honest way to read the print: the duty windfall is noise; the 18% underlying growth into the Diwali season is the signal - the season that, thirty years ago, taught a failing boutique what Indian customers actually buy.

The scene that deserves the last word is Basel, 1996. M S Shantharam walks a trade-show floor, stops at a spectrometer built for metallurgy labs, and sees what nobody in a centuries-old industry had productized: proof. The machine cost over Rs 10 lakh at a time the business buying it was losing money; the industry it was aimed at would respond with threats; the customers it served would first respond with tears. Titan bought it anyway, reprogrammed it for forty-five alloys, put it in the window - and then, when proof alone failed to sell a single extra bangle, did the harder thing and underwrote the answer with its own balance sheet. Plenty of companies find the indictment. The ones that matter build the remedy.

Sources read in full for this piece: Tata’s heritage and 40-year histories, C K Venkataraman’s excerpted account on Rediff, Vinay Kamath’s excerpted account on NDTV Profit, the 2016 CaratLane filing via Business Standard, and Thursday’s results coverage in Hindu BusinessLine, Mint and Business Today. Nothing on this page is investment advice.

33.title: The biscuit with no founder
33.fact: A Slow Burn long read, Saturday 7 November 2026. On Friday, Britannia Industries reported its biggest-ever quarterly revenue - Rs 5,542 crore, up 16.6% - and the market sold the stock down 4.2%. The company behind that print is 134 years old, was started by founders whose names nobody recorded, and has passed through at least seven sets of owners: an Englishman in a Calcutta house, the Gupta brothers of Dum Dum, a Biscuit King who died in Tihar Jail, a French dairy giant, and the Wadias, who won it in a boardroom war and still run it today. This is the story of how a Rs 295 bakery became a machine that sells biscuits in more than eighty countries - and what Friday's verdict says about what that machine is now worth.

groups.heading: 1. The company with no known founder

blocks.html: Britannia begins with a hole in the record. Sometime in 1892, in a house in Calcutta, a group of English businessmen started a biscuit company with an investment of Rs 295. Their names are not preserved; even the company's own centenary coverage describes the founders as unknown (Business Today's centenary account). What is recorded is what happened next: in 1897 the Gupta brothers acquired the operation and ran it as V.S. Brothers from Dum Dum, and in 1918 an English businessman named C.H. Holmes took it on as a partner, folding it into what became the Britannia Biscuit Company.

The new company industrialized fast. In 1921 it imported gas-fired ovens - among the first of their kind east of Suez - replacing wood-fired baking, and in 1924 it became a subsidiary of Peek Frean, the British biscuit giant, tying the Calcutta bakery to a global supply of recipes, machinery and standards. Then came the war. Through the Second World War, Britannia's factories ran at up to 95% of capacity making biscuits for the British Indian Army - the contract that turned a colonial bakery into an industrial operation with national reach (Business Today). The pattern that would define the next century was already set: the owners would keep changing, and the machine would keep running.

Independent India kept reshuffling the register. In 1975 the Parry's group took over distribution; in 1978 the company went public, with Indian shareholding rising above 60%; in 1979 it took its modern name, Britannia Industries; and by 1983 sales crossed Rs 100 crore (Business Today). The business was solid, staid and leaderless in ambition - exactly the kind of asset a raider looks for. The raider arrived in 1981, and he arrived through potato chips.

Rajan Pillai was a Kerala-born commodities trader who had built a snacks business in Singapore - the Ole chips brand - and parlayed it into a stake of about 5% in Britannia. His ambitions were never really about India alone. Through the 1980s he assembled a chain of biscuit companies across Asia: a stake in Associated Biscuits, alliances and deals that ran through Ross Johnson's RJR Nabisco and the French group BSN - the company the world would later know as Danone. When the American buyout firm KKR took over RJR Nabisco in 1988 in the era's defining leveraged buyout, the pieces shifted again, and by 1989 Pillai controlled six Asian biscuit companies worth over $400 million. The press gave him the title he had wanted: the Biscuit King (Business Standard's retrospective).

groups.heading: 3. The fall of the Biscuit King

blocks.html: The empire was leveraged, and the alliances were conditional. In 1993 the ground gave way: Nusli Wadia - the Bombay Dyeing industrialist who had long wanted Britannia - moved on the company in alliance with the very partner Pillai believed was his, Danone. It was, by the accounts of the time, a hostile takeover. The wound that cut deepest was personal: Pillai's own lieutenant, Sunil Alagh - the manager who ran Britannia day to day - switched sides and stayed on under the new owners. Pillai lost the company he had spent a decade assembling (Business Standard).

What followed was one of the starkest falls in Indian business history. Pursued by Singapore on cheating charges, Pillai fought extradition from India; in 1995, while being held in Delhi's Tihar Jail awaiting the outcome, he died of liver cirrhosis. He was 47. The man who had named himself the Biscuit King did not live to see what his former partners would build on his foundation - or to see them turn on each other (Business Standard).

The 1993 victors structured Britannia as a 50:50 partnership: the Wadias and Danone held the company jointly through a web of entities, together controlling just over half. For a decade the arrangement worked. Then it curdled. The first public crack came in June 2003, when the chief executive - Sunil Alagh, the same lieutenant who had defected from Pillai a decade earlier - was sacked over alleged misuse of company funds. The deeper fight was over Tiger. Britannia's mass-market glucose biscuit was the company's most valuable brand in volume terms, and it emerged in 2006-07 that Danone had registered the Tiger trademark in some seventy countries - with about forty-five granted, from Indonesia and Egypt to Malaysia, Singapore and Pakistan - without Britannia's consent (Times of India's account of the confrontation). To the Wadias, a partner quietly taking ownership of their best brand across Asia was not a partner.

The confrontation peaked at the 2007 annual general meeting, in full view of shareholders. Danone wanted its biscuits business consolidated; Wadia made his price the sticking point, delivering the line that settled the argument's terms: everything was available - "at my price." Danone's side answered with its own tell: the group, its representatives acknowledged, was no longer in the biscuit business anywhere in the world except India, having sold its global biscuits arm to Kraft. A partner with no biscuits elsewhere and a trademark portfolio in forty-five countries was, in the Wadias' reading, a partner preparing either to leave or to take. It left. In April 2009 Danone sold its holding to the Wadia side, ending the joint venture and leaving the family in sole control - through every registry, about 50.96% of a company that had now outlasted every owner who ever touched it (Times of India).

What the Wadias did next is the reason this is a business story and not only a saga: they hired operators and let them run. The defining hire was Vinita Bali in 2005. She was a global marketer - a worldwide marketing director at Coca-Cola in Atlanta under Sergio Zyman, with stints at Cadbury across Nigeria, South Africa and the UK, where she had run the Wispa launch - and she took the job after her mother's stroke brought her back to India (Hindu BusinessLine's profile; Forbes). Bali rebuilt Britannia around six power brands - Tiger, Good Day, Milk Bikis, 50-50, Marie and Treat - pushed Rs 5 packs, took trans fats out of the recipes, and lifted growth from 9% to 22%. The detail that captures the era: a visit to a Delhi factory, where cartons of fortified biscuits bound for the World Food Programme made the case that a biscuit company could sell nutrition, not just snacks; by 2008 Bill Gates was citing Britannia in his "creative capitalism" argument. Her own summary of how she sorted people was three words: "great, good and gone" (Forbes).

After Bali came a decade of professional succession: Varun Berry, a PepsiCo and Hindustan Unilever veteran who joined in 2013 as chief operating officer, ran the company for thirteen years through its most profitable stretch before resigning in November 2025 (Business Standard); a brief interlude under Rajneet Kohli ended in March 2025; the chief executive's office today belongs to Rakshit Hargave, who holds the title of CEO and Managing Director (the company's own site). The company the professionals run now sells in more than eighty countries.

Which brings the story to Friday. In the September 2026 quarter, reported midday Friday, Britannia's consolidated revenue rose 16.6% to Rs 5,542 crore - the biggest quarterly revenue in its 134 years - with operating profit up 8.5% to Rs 943 crore and profit attributable to owners up 10.2% to Rs 721 crore; general trade, its oldest channel, grew at 2.6 times its FY26 level (Business Today, from the results and investor presentation). The market's verdict, delivered in the same session: the stock fell 4.2% to Rs 4,790 on the BSE. The scene is worth sitting with. A company started by founders so unimportant to memory that nobody wrote down their names; fought over by a king who died in jail and a family that outwaited the French; professionalized until its biscuits rode the World Food Programme's trucks - that company posted its best revenue ever, and the tape asked for more. Nusli Wadia's 2007 line survives as the machine's own question: everything has a price. The market spends every session deciding whether Rs 4,790 a share is his price, or its own.

Sources read in full for this piece: Business Today's centenary account and its Friday results coverage, Business Standard's retrospectives on Rajan Pillai and Varun Berry's resignation, Hindu BusinessLine's profile of Vinita Bali, Forbes' 2012 Tough Cookie profile, the Times of India's reporting on the 2007 AGM confrontation, and Britannia's own about-us page for current leadership. Prices are BSE official closes. Nothing on this page is investment advice.

34.title: The bhujia that said no
34.fact: A Slow Burn long read, Sunday 8 November 2026 - Diwali. This evening, a large share of India's Diwali tables will hold something made by Haldiram's. The company behind the packet is a family business that began as a boy's sideline in Bikaner, split itself into warring territories, refused PepsiCo's cheque, reunited its two biggest branches last year, and sold a 9% stake to Singapore's Temasek at a valuation of Rs 84,000 crore. An IPO is the stated next step. This is how a bhujia shop became a $10-billion company without ever selling the shop.
34.intro: The founding date itself is contested - 1918 by one account, 1937 by another - and the family split the map of India between cousins to keep the peace. It did not work. What worked was saying no: to debt, to PepsiCo, to every suitor who wanted the name.

blocks.html: Bikaner's old city has a market lane named for a snack. Bhujia Bazaar, inside the larger Bara Bazaar, is where the crisp fried strands made from moth-bean flour became a craft, and it is home to what is remembered as the first Haldiram store, from the early 1920s (The National's Bikaner dispatch). The man the brand is named for, Ganga Bishan Agarwal - Haldiram Ji - was a boy working in the family shop when he started tinkering with the recipe. The founding year is the first thing the record cannot agree on, and this read names the disagreement rather than picking: Pavitra Kumar's family biography Bhujia Barons traces his first sales to 1918, a date Forbes India's profile repeats; Business Standard's account puts the first venture in 1919; the company's formal shop is dated 1937 by Financial Express and Outlook Business. The likely shape of the truth is a boy's sideline around 1918-19 hardening into a real shop years later - but the sources say what they say.

What the boy changed was the ingredient. Bhujia was made from besan - chickpea flour. Ganga Bishan made his from moth ki dal, a drought-resistant desert bean, finer and crisper, and Bikaner noticed overnight (Forbes India). He priced it up, not down: five paise a kilo against the two paise his grandfather Bhikharam charged, because dearer meant exclusive, and he named it Dungar Sev after the reigning Maharaja Dungar Singh - a royal endorsement borrowed before marketing had a name for itself. By the early 1930s the price had climbed from two paise to twenty-five, and the whole family lived off it (Forbes India). A century later, Bikaner still buys its bhujia fresh: makers like Rewat Ram start at 5 AM and fry two quintals a day, and no local will buy a packet made yesterday (The National). The packaged giant grew out of a craft that refuses, to this day, to be packaged.

The family's answer to ambition was geography. In the early 1950s Ganga Bishan and his sons opened in Kolkata - Haldiram Bhujiawala, later split into Haldiram's Prabhuji and Haldiram; Forbes India names the sons Moolchand and Rameshwar Lal, while Business Standard's account says Satyanarayan and Rameshwarlal. To stop the branches from eating each other, Ganga Bishan imposed a territorial settlement: each line of the family got its own map, and West Bengal went to Rameshwar Lal's. Over the following decades Moolchand's sons fanned out - Shiv Kishan to Nagpur, and later Manohar Lal and Madhusudan to Delhi, while Shiv Ratan stayed in Bikaner and eventually built Bikaji (The National; Forbes India). The borders held on paper and failed in practice. In 1991 the Kolkata family entered Delhi and refused to change its branding; the trademark case ran almost fifteen years, until Delhi's Haldiram's won sole ownership of the Haldiram Bhujiawala mark in 2013 (Forbes India).

The settlement left three unequal kingdoms. By 2023, on Business Standard's reporting, the Delhi unit under Manohar Lal and Madhusudan Agarwal was the revenue leader at about Rs 5,000 crore, Shiv Kishan's Nagpur unit stood second at roughly Rs 4,000 crore, and the Bikaner line third at about Rs 1,600 crore (Business Standard). Three companies, one name, and a customer who never knew which cousin's bhujia was in the packet - an arrangement that kept the peace, capped the ambition, and made an eventual reunion almost compulsory.

The Delhi branch began as a rebellion. Manohar Lal and Madhusudan, the youngest sons of Moolchand, fought their father for the right to strike out; the family was opposed to debt on principle, so Manohar Lal and his older brother Shiv Kishan withdrew all their hard-earned savings to fund the move. Business began in 1983 in Chandni Chowk, where bhujia was nobody's novelty - Ghantewala and Bikanervala were entrenched - and the newcomers fought back with flavour tweaks and relentless distribution until they broke even (Forbes India). Then came 1984: the shop and the family apartment above it burned in the anti-Sikh riots. Manohar Lal sent his family back to Bikaner and rebuilt with Madhusudan, brick by brick; once business picked up again, the family turned its apartment into a factory overnight and pulled long sleepless nights to keep up with demand (Forbes India).

What Manohar Lal brought that his grandfather's generation resisted was process. He pushed production in-house against the objection that it was needless expense, and he replaced stamped polythene with branded, higher-grade packaging over similar protests (Outlook Business). Both defiances became the brand's spine: hygiene nobody could see and a packet everybody recognized. The first proper factory came in the late 1980s; distribution became the Delhi branch's signature weapon, to the point that the Rs 5 bhujia packet circulated at railway stalls as a substitute for loose change (Forbes India). The lesson the family still quotes is organic growth - no loans, no shortcuts, one city at a time.

When PepsiCo came knocking in the early 1990s, Haldiram said no. Liberalisation had just opened the door to every global brand, and an offer to buy out the country's best-known snack name made obvious sense on paper. Manohar Lal Agarwal's answer, recalled in Bhujia Barons, settled the company's character in one line: I refused to give up our brand, our dream (Outlook Business). PepsiCo launched its own Indian snack brand, Lehar, instead. It never came close. The pattern repeated for three decades: Kellogg's weighed a partnership or stake at a $3-billion valuation around 2019 (Forbes India); in 2023 Reuters reported Tata Group talks for at least 51% - a majority, the thing the family had always refused - which Tata Consumer publicly denied (Business Standard); and in May 2024 a Blackstone-led group's bid for a majority stake, valuing the firm above $8 billion (Times of India, May 2024), went nowhere - the wooing never became a deal, because the promoters had decided internally to keep the majority inside the family (Times of India, March 2025).

The refusal was affordable because the machine kept compounding. In 2013-14 Haldiram's Rs 3,500-crore revenue exceeded the combined India revenues of PepsiCo and McDonald's (Outlook Business). Between 2020-21 and 2022-23, revenue from operations grew 46%, from Rs 7,151 crore to Rs 10,479 crore, while profit rose 47% to cross Rs 1,000 crore, per Tofler data cited by Outlook. In FY24 the combined business posted about Rs 12,800 crore of revenue and roughly Rs 1,400 crore of net profit - an 18% five-year CAGR - on an estimated 13% share of the organised savoury-snacks market, with namkeens contributing about 60% of revenue (Financial Express). Frost & Sullivan's narrower count of the organised traditional-snacks market - Rs 17,900 crore in 2022-23 - gives Haldiram's a 40% share (Outlook Business). The company sells in over 100 countries today on Outlook Business's count - Financial Express puts the footprint at over 80 - from samosas that flew to space with Sunita Williams to the 400-product catalogue; exports are still only about a tenth of the business, and most of that is the diaspora buying a taste of home (Outlook Business; Financial Express).

groups.heading: 5. The reunion, and the next refusal

blocks.html: Last year the map finally folded. After year-long negotiations, the Delhi and Nagpur branches merged into a single entity - named Haldiram Snacks Food by Outlook Business, and Haldiram Foods and Snacks Private Limited in TOI's reporting - in which the Delhi family holds 56% and the Nagpur family 44% (Outlook Business; Times of India). Into that merged company came the first outsider money the family had ever accepted: Temasek, Singapore's state investment firm, took 9% for about $1 billion at a valuation of Rs 84,000 crore, with a board seat; Alpha Wave Global and Abu Dhabi's International Holding Company together hold about 6% more (Times of India; Outlook Business). At roughly $10 billion, the valuation puts a bhujia maker in the company of Dabur and Tata Consumer - and Temasek's cheque, among the largest private-equity deals in Indian consumer history, was rare precisely because global investors almost never back unlisted family firms (Outlook Business).

Which sets up the decision this generation of Agrawals now owns. The stated plan is an IPO: the merger was structured for it, the Temasek price gives it a public benchmark, and advisers talk about governance, integration and supply chains with the fluency of a pre-listing house (Times of India; Outlook Business). The family that refused PepsiCo's whole cheque accepted Singapore's small one - 9%, not 51%, board seat included - and the bet underneath that choice is the same bet the boy in Bhujia Bazaar made when he doubled his grandfather's price: that the name is worth more than the money. A public listing will test it quarterly, in the open, forever. The shop said no for a hundred years. The next answer is due soon.

Sources read in full for this piece: Forbes India's 2019 profile of the family, Business Standard's 2023 account of the family disputes and the Tata talks, Financial Express's August 2025 business profile, the Times of India's March 2025 reporting of the Temasek deal and the merger, Outlook Business's December 2025 cover profile, The National's 2023 dispatch from Bikaner's Bhujia Bazaar, and the company's own about-us page. Founding dates conflict across sources - 1918, 1919 and 1937 are all named in the text where they appear. The Temasek stake is carried at 9% per the deal reporting; one profile rounds it to 10%.

35.title: The app that outgrew its name
35.fact: A Slow Burn long read, Monday 9 November 2026. In March 2025, shareholders of Zomato - the food-delivery app on a hundred million Indian phones - voted to rename the company Eternal. The app kept its name; the company had outgrown it. Ten months later the founder who scanned the first menu walked out of the CEO's office and handed the keys to the founder of the company he had bought. This is how a menu box became a listed giant, crashed 72% from its peak, bet itself on ten-minute groceries, and changed its name and its chief within a year.
35.intro: The record on this one is unusually well-lit: the company writes shareholder letters meant to be read, the founder explains himself in public, and the numbers - from the Rs 46 low to the Rs 4,447-crore acquisition - sit in exchange filings. The story still holds one genuine surprise: who ended up running it.

blocks.html: The idea began as an office irritation. Deepinder Goyal and Pankaj Chaddah were analysts at Bain & Company in Delhi when they noticed how hard it was to find a restaurant menu - you walked to the restaurant, or you asked a friend who had kept one. In 2008 they started scanning menus and putting them online, and called the site Foodiebay (YourStory's history). It was a sideline run from a consulting desk, and it was not Goyal's first try - an earlier venture, foodlet.com, had aimed to carry restaurant promotions and online ordering, and was folded into the newer idea.

Two years later the sideline won. In 2010 Foodiebay renamed itself Zomato - derived from tomato, the company said, with a zing added for recall - the founders went full-time, and an engineer named Gunjan Patidar joined as the technology spine; Info Edge, which had backed the young company, blessed the new name as one that could carry further (YourStory). The renaming was the first appearance of a pattern that runs through the whole story: this company changes its name when its ambition outgrows the old one. It would happen again, bigger, fifteen years later.

The early Zomato was a search engine with legs. By 2011 it was India's default for restaurant discovery, and it had already tried and shelved a side business - event ticketing - a first lesson in focus (YourStory). In 2012 came the apps and the borders: Android and iOS, then the UAE, Sri Lanka, Qatar, Britain, the Philippines, South Africa. The funding followed the map - $16.7 million from Info Edge in 2013, then $37 million from Sequoia and Info Edge, then $60 million in 2014 at a $660-million valuation - and the company bought its way into new territories: Menu-mania in New Zealand, Gastronauci in Poland, Cibando in Italy, and in 2015 the Seattle-based Urbanspoon for an estimated $60 million.

The harder pivot came the same year: food delivery, in 2015 - turning a company that told you where to eat into one that brought the food. The transition carried the decade's scars. A data breach in 2015, resolved in twelve hours, was the first public roadblock. Chaddah, the co-founder who had scanned the first menus, left in 2018. The delivery war against Swiggy burned cash for years, and Zomato later elevated the lieutenants of that war - Gaurav Gupta, Mohit Gupta, Akriti Chopra - to co-founder status, the title used as a war decoration (YourStory). In January 2020 Zomato absorbed Uber Eats' India business in an all-stock deal that left Uber with a tenth of the combined company - the first time the market saw the move that would define it: buy the competitor with paper, keep building.

On 23 July 2021, Zomato became the first of India's internet unicorns to list. The IPO - open 14 to 16 July, priced at Rs 72-76 a share - was subscribed more than 38 times; the stock opened at Rs 116 on the NSE, touched Rs 138, and closed its first day at Rs 125, up 66%, at a market value of about Rs 98,000 crore - more, that day, than 76-year-old Tata Motors (YourStory). The bell was rung digitally by the company's delivery riders. It was the coming-out party for an entire sector. The top, though, was still four months away: the stock peaked at Rs 169.10 on 16 November 2021, 35% above its listing-day close (Business Today, on the peak date).

A year later the bill came due. Zomato had never posted a profit, rates were rising, and the market had stopped paying for growth stories. Then the mechanics turned brutal: on 25 July 2022, the one-year lock-in on pre-IPO shares expired, 613 crore shares became sellable, and the stock plunged 14% to a record low of Rs 46 - down about 72% from its peak of Rs 169.10, and 38% below the price the public had paid at listing (Economic Times). A founder's paper fortune, a sector's flagship, and a generation's first tech IPO all sat underwater at once.

The defining move had actually been made a month before the low. On 24 June 2022, with its own stock at Rs 70.35, Zomato's board approved the acquisition of Blinkit - the ten-minute grocery delivery startup, formerly Grofers, itself bleeding cash - for Rs 4,447 crore, paid entirely in stock: up to 629 million new shares, 6.88% of the company, at Rs 70.76 apiece (Mint, on the deal). The market's verdict was swift and hostile - analysts said the deal would hurt the path to profitability, and the stock's slide to Rs 46 began within weeks. Goyal bought a burning company with depressed paper, at the exact moment the market trusted him least.

Inside the numbers, the bet was a swap: Zomato's slowing food-delivery growth for a stake in the one category growing faster - instant delivery of everything else. Blinkit's founder, Albinder Dhindsa, kept running it with the autonomy Zomato's business chiefs always had. The deal's structure left the old Grofers backers - SoftBank, Tiger Global - holding Zomato paper instead. What nobody could know at Rs 46 was that the acquired founder would end up running the whole company.

groups.heading: 5. The turn, and the new name

blocks.html: The turn arrived quietly, in a single line. On 3 August 2023 Zomato reported its first-ever profit: Rs 2 crore, on revenue of Rs 2,416 crore, up 71% on the year. Two crore rupees is a rounding error in a company that size - and the most important number it had ever printed, because the question hanging over it since listing had never been how fast it could grow, but whether the model could make money at all. Blinkit followed the same arc: from a Rs 156-crore adjusted quarterly loss in the year-ago quarter to a Rs 184-crore adjusted profit in the quarter just reported, under the man who came with the deal.

By early 2025 the name was the only thing that hadn't caught up. Internally, the company had started calling itself Eternal when it acquired Blinkit, to tell the company apart from the app; the public rename, Goyal wrote, was always meant to come the day something beyond Zomato became a significant driver of the future. With Blinkit, that day had come. On 10 March 2025 shareholders approved the change - 99.75% of votes in favour - and Zomato the company became Eternal Ltd, housing four businesses: the Zomato app, Blinkit, the going-out vertical District, and the B2B supplier Hyperpure (moneycontrol). The app on your phone never changed. The company on the stock exchange had outgrown it.

On 21 January 2026, Goyal published the letter nobody expected. He was stepping down as Group CEO to explore new ideas - "the kinds of ideas that are better pursued outside a public company," involving "significantly higher-risk exploration and experimentation." The expectations of a public-company CEO in India, he wrote, demand singular focus, and Eternal deserved to stay focused and disciplined (the full letter, via NDTV). His successor: Albinder Dhindsa - the Blinkit founder he had acquired three and a half years earlier. "Blinkit's journey from acquisition to breakeven happened under his leadership," the letter says. "He has the DNA of a battle-hardened founder and his ability to execute far exceeds mine." And the sentence the whole story turns on: "I have spent eighteen years, almost half my life, building this company. I will continue doing that." Goyal stayed as vice chairman - strategy, culture, governance - but the operating centre of gravity moved, by his own design, to the man he bought.

The machine the new CEO inherited is running hot. Last quarter Eternal's revenue rose 78% to Rs 24,138 crore, profit nearly doubled to Rs 125 crore - and still missed the street's estimate, because expenses rose 75% with it (Mint, on the results). Blinkit added 308 stores in the quarter, raised its target to 3,500 by March 2027, and turned in Rs 184 crore of adjusted profit. Goyal, meanwhile, is doing exactly what the letter promised: his new venture, Temple - an Rs 85,000 brain-monitoring wearable he says he has put $20 million of his own money into - spent last week being called a scam by doctors online, and he spent it calling the science defensible (India Today). Higher risk, indeed.

The decision scene is the handover itself, because of who stood on each side of it. Founders who outgrow their first act usually sell, or stay too long. Goyal did the third thing: he bought his successor's company at the market's darkest moment, gave him room to prove the bet, renamed the company for the future the bet created - and then, by his own account, handed him the keys because the bought founder executes better than the buying one. Eighteen years from a scanned menu to a $35-billion company, and the last lesson of the story is the first one, repeated: when the ambition outgrows the name, change the name. When the company outgrows the founder, change that too.

Sources read in full for this piece: YourStory's 2021 history from Foodiebay to the listing; Mint on the Blinkit acquisition and on Eternal's September-quarter results; Economic Times on the July 2022 record low; moneycontrol on the Eternal rename; NDTV's full text of Goyal's January 2026 letter; India Today on the Temple controversy; Reuters, Business Standard and Financial Express headlines corroborating the stepdown and the first profit. Founding dates do not conflict across sources (2008, renamed 2010). The Blinkit share-issue price and stake are from the deal's regulatory filing as reported. The $35-billion figure for the company's value is Goyal's own, from his public posts.

36.title: The chemist's customer
36.fact: A Slow Burn long read, Tuesday 10 November 2026. On Monday, Divi's Laboratories touched a record high of Rs 11,818 and entered the Rs 3-trillion market-cap club, after a September quarter with profit up 64%. Thirty-six years earlier, its founder had walked out of another man's company on a morning when a hundred and twenty-five employees resigned with him. Murali Divi failed his twelfth standard, failed his first year of pharmacy, went to America with seven dollars, came home, built India's first USFDA-approved ingredient plant for someone else - and then built one for himself on a single rule: never compete with the customer. When an American regulator shut down his factory in 2017, the world's biggest drug companies went to plead for their supplier. This is how that company was made.
36.intro: The record here runs through long interviews the founder gave Forbes India and the Times of India a decade apart, the exchange filings behind the 2017 import alert, and this week's results. Where the two profiles disagree - a return in 1983 or 1984, an alert lifted in six months or eight - this piece says so and keeps both.

blocks.html: The story's first fact is a failed exam. Murali Krishna Prasad Divi, from an agrarian family in Machilipatnam, Andhra Pradesh, failed his twelfth standard - and then failed his first year of BPharm too (Times of India, 2024). What followed the second failure is the part the legend leaves out: he came back and finished the degree with distinction, added an MPharm, and in 1975 joined Warner Hindustan as a trainee. From there he moved to Uniloids - the first venture of a chemist named Kallam Anji Reddy, who had just quit the state-owned Indian Drugs and Pharmaceuticals to turn entrepreneur. The two would spend the next decade and a half orbiting each other.

Restless, Divi left for the United States with seven dollars in his pocket - "in those days that was all the foreign exchange you could carry abroad," he told TOI. He had earned his doctorate in pharmaceutical sciences from Kakatiya University before leaving, then spent years in American pharma and fine-chemicals research, in senior R&D roles at firms including Fike Chemical (Forbes India, 2014). Then home pulled him back: a family emergency and homesickness, per TOI's account, which dates the return to 1983; Forbes India says 1984. Both profiles agree on what happened next - he reconnected with Anji Reddy, worked briefly as general manager of R&D at Reddy's Standard Organics, and in 1984 joined the newly formed Dr Reddy's Laboratories as a director. The two men went looking for a sick company to fix.

They found Cheminor Drugs - a contract manufacturer so sick it had eight reactors and six employees. "When we took it over, people laughed," Divi recalled years later, in a memory published on Dr Reddy's own website. "They said, 'This guy comes from the US. Dr Anji Reddy and Murali think they can make it like IDPL.' We kept quiet. Of course, we turned it around" (Forbes India). The division of labour was clean: Reddy ran business development; Divi, as managing director, ran everything technical. He hired fresh graduates - Ramesh Babu Potluri, TVVSN Murthy, NV Ramana, G Hemanth Kumar - and personally trained them in the chemistry.

The target was ibuprofen, the pain drug. Within a year the team had a cost-effective manufacturing process; the line scaled to 1,200 tonnes a year, about a quarter of the world's demand, and Cheminor became India's first active-ingredient plant to win USFDA approval - first for ibuprofen, later for the antacid ranitidine (TOI). Divi's style was total: at the office by 7:30 in the morning, at the plant until midnight, visiting junior employees' homes when they had problems, Potluri - later founder of SMS Pharma - told Forbes India. That detail matters, because of what it made possible in 1990.

groups.heading: 3. The morning a hundred and twenty-five people quit

blocks.html: By 1990 the partnership had curdled. The next generation of the Reddy family was being inducted into the company and questioned Divi's decisions; egos clashed, Potluri says. Divi left. And on the day he left Cheminor, almost a hundred and twenty-five people resigned with him (Forbes India). It is one of the great walkouts in Indian corporate history, and it was not a raid - he had no factory to take them to. They followed the chemist, not the payroll. Asked by Forbes India why he quit, Divi gave the answer that frames everything after: "Perhaps because I was destined to become chairman of my own company rather than remaining managing director elsewhere."

What he founded in 1990 was not yet a manufacturer. Divi's Research Centre was a consulting shop: Divi and his chemists engineered better processes for making drug ingredients and sold the processes to the highest bidder. Several of the chemists from the walkout eventually built their own companies - TVVSN Murthy became managing director of Potluri's SMS Pharma; others, like NV Ramana and Hemanth Kumar, joined Divi's a few years later. Ramana is still there, an executive director. The consulting years taught the company's permanent lesson: your process knowledge is worth more than your plant, and the customer you enable today is the customer who must never fear you tomorrow.

The decision scene is 1994. Divi took roughly Rs 7 crore of his own savings and committed to a greenfield ingredient plant in Nalgonda that would cost Rs 71 crore - ten rupees of project for every rupee he had - and rechristened the company Divi's Laboratories (TOI). "I borrowed only when I started the company," he said. "I borrowed Rs 35 crore from IDBI in 1995, paid it back in nearly five years. We also stopped working-capital borrowings since 2010." By 1995 the company had a seventy-one-acre manufacturing facility in Hyderabad staffed with chemists Divi had trained at Cheminor (Forbes India) - the two profiles describe the build-out from their own reporting, the Nalgonda greenfield in TOI's account and the Hyderabad base in Forbes India's.

The rules he set then still govern the company. No formulations - Divi's would make the ingredients, never the finished tablets, because making the product would turn the company from its customers' supplier into their competitor. No patent challenges, no litigation with big pharma, at a time when the rest of Indian pharma was building fortunes on exactly that. "From the very beginning we decided to not get into litigation with big pharma," Divi told TOI. "We never violate patents and we don't compete with our customers." His son Kiran Divi, now CEO, puts the commercial theology plainly: "Customers are gods. Gods don't bargain. We work with eight of the top ten pharma companies in the world." The company listed in 2003 at Rs 140 a share - a Rs 45-crore IPO with an offer for sale - with the family holding about 52% today.

The rule's strangest proof came in 2017, when the machine broke. That March, the US Food and Drug Administration hit Divi's unit-II at Visakhapatnam with import alerts under clauses 99-32 and 66-40 for good-manufacturing-practice non-compliance, followed by a warning letter - the regulator's most serious toolkit, "detention without physical examination" (Hindu BusinessLine, on the filings). For an ingredient maker, an import alert is a death sentence on a delay: your customers' production lines run on your shipments. And here the legend earns its place. Pharma folklore, as TOI tells it, has several big-pharma customers dashing to the USFDA's office to get the issue resolved - because Divi's was their largest supplier of ingredients for naproxen, dextromethorphan, gabapentin and levetiracetam. The regulator granted exemptions for key products while the fix proceeded. In July the 99-32 alert was lifted; in early November the warning letter was closed out; on 14 November 2017 the remaining alert was removed. That is eight months from March to November on the filings' own dates; TOI's telling calls it six months, "perhaps the shortest ever" - this piece keeps the filings' calendar and notes the profile's. Either way, the point stands: when Divi's plant stopped, the world's biggest drug companies treated it as their own emergency. The customer had become the hostage of the relationship - exactly as designed.

groups.heading: 6. The second generation, and the next molecule

blocks.html: The company Murali Divi now chairs is in its second generation. Kiran Divi joined in August 2001 and has been CEO since January 2020, overseeing operations and corporate functions; Nilima Prasad Divi is whole-time director for commercial matters; Nimmagadda Venkata Ramana - the NV Ramana of the walkout - an executive director since October 1994, runs strategy, sales and custom manufacturing (the company's leadership page). The founder, in his seventies, still insists his main business is running farms and growing orchards (Forbes India). The balance sheet carries the old disciplines: debt-free, about Rs 4,000 crore of cash as of 2024, no working-capital borrowings since 2010. The Covid years added the one speculative chapter - a windfall making the antiviral Molnupiravir's ingredients took the stock to Rs 5,425 in October 2021 and the family's wealth to about Rs 75,000 crore (TOI) - and then the windfall left, as windfalls do.

What replaced it is the reason the stock touched a record Rs 11,818 this Monday and entered the Rs 3-trillion club, up 105% from its April low. The September quarter: profit up 64% to Rs 1,127 crore on revenue up 35% to Rs 3,676 crore, with custom synthesis - making ingredients for specific customers' new drugs - up 44% to Rs 2,200 crore on shipped validation batches, margins at 42.6%, the highest since the Covid era (Economic Times, on the results; Business Standard). Three large dedicated projects are in validation, one nearing commercialisation; three new projects of Rs 650-700 crore each are expected to be commercialised from the second half of this fiscal year into FY28 (Business Standard, on the brokerages’ read). And the next molecule is the world's most contested: the company is building peptide capacity, including the chemistry behind GLP-1 obesity drugs - the next blockbuster class for the same big-pharma customers it has never once competed with (TOI; Businessworld).

The story ends where it began: with the chemistry and the rule. A failed student became a chemist good enough that a hundred and twenty-five people quit their jobs to follow him into a consulting shop. The shop became a plant on a ten-to-one bet. The plant became the supplier the world's biggest drug companies could not afford to lose - loyal not through contracts but through abstinence: three decades of refusing to make the final pill. In an industry built on challenging patents, Divi's Laboratories compounded by declining to fight its customers. "We mastered the chemistry," the founder says, "to an extent that it's very difficult for others to enter into our products." The record high this week is the market, thirty years on, agreeing.

Sources read in full for this piece: Forbes India's 2014 profile "Murali Divi: The Accidental Chemist"; the Times of India's 2024 profile "How 12th fail teen turned Hyderabad's richest businessman"; Business Standard on the September-quarter results and the Rs 3-trillion market cap; Economic Times on the results; Hindu BusinessLine on the 2017 USFDA import alert and its lifting; BW Businessworld's 2023 interview; the company's own leadership page; and Monday's record-high alerts. Two conflicts are named in the text and kept: the return from the US (1983 in TOI, 1984 in Forbes India) and the import alert's duration (eight months on the filings' dates, "six months" in TOI's telling). Prices and percentages are BSE official prints; the Rs 4,000-crore cash is as reported in 2024; the roughly 52% family stake is per the company's September 2026 shareholding-pattern filing.

37.title: The man who would not split
37.fact: A Slow Burn long read, Wednesday 11 November 2026. On Tuesday, with the market shut for a holiday, MRF's board declared a Rs 3 dividend on a quarter where profit fell 27% on the filing's own headline line - a footnote in the life of a company that began in 1946 as a twenty-three-paise balloon in a rented shed, after a princely state destroyed the founder's family bank. K.M. Mammen Mappillai drove the multinationals out of tread rubber, sold tyres to the Americans, fought off Michelin's grab for control, and never once split the stock. One share now costs Rs 1,25,070.85. This is how the machine was built.
37.intro: Six chapters: the ruin, the shed, the pivot, the tyres, the sieges, and the ledger. All prices are BSE official prints; the founding-date conflict is named where it lives.

blocks.html: The story of India's largest tyre company begins with the destruction of a bank. Kandathil Mammen Mammen Mappillai was born in 1922 into the Kandathil family of Kerala - owners of the Malayala Manorama newspaper, a family that would collect five Padma awards across its generations. His father, K.C. Mammen Mappillai, ran the family's flagship, the Travancore National and Quilon Bank, and ran it into a feud with Sir C.P. Ramaswami Iyer, the autocratic Dewan of the princely state of Travancore. In 1938 the state liquidated the bank, and the father went to jail. The son, sixteen that year, finished his education at Madras Christian College sleeping on the bare floorboards of St. Thomas Hall (Mint's profile of the founder carries the details).

Every empire has its founding humiliation; this one had a family honour to reclaim. When Mammen Mappillai set up his tiny unit in a rented shed in Tiruvottiyur, on the coast of north Madras, in 1946, he was, in Mint's phrase, building less a company than a restoration. The capital was Rs 10,000. The product was a toy balloon that sold for twenty-three paise.

Tiruvottiyur was then part of Madras's auto belt, a neighbourhood of small workshops and fishermen. In the shed, Mappillai and his wife - Meera Kunjamma, a chemist by training, later described as MRF's first employee - made toy balloons by hand, and he took them out to sell (Forbes India). By 1949 the shed was turning out latex-cast squeaking toys, industrial gloves and contraceptives, and the business took its first office at 334, Thambu Chetty Street in the city's old commercial quarter (the company's own milestones). One note on dates: the company, the Economic Times' corporate history and every older account date the founding to 1946; a 2023 NDTV Profit profile dates it to 1949, which is when the product range widened. This paper carries the company's own year.

The name was the address of the ambition: Madras Rubber Factory. There were no machines yet - the "factory" of the late forties was a shed with workers' hands. But the science graduate and the chemist were learning rubber: how latex cures, how a compound behaves, what makes one batch squeak and another crack. When the pivot came, they were ready for it.

In 1952 Mappillai noticed something in his own family: a cousin ran tyre-retreading plants, and the tread rubber those plants consumed - the strip of fresh rubber vulcanised onto a worn tyre to give it a second life - was imported (Mint). He installed the shed's first machine, a rubber mill, and began making tread rubber. The multinationals who owned India's rubber market - Dunlop, Goodyear, Firestone - treated the Indian entrant as a curiosity.

Four years later they were gone from the segment. By 1955 Madras Rubber Factory was the only Indian-owned unit making the superior extruded, non-blooming, cushion-backed tread rubber (ET's corporate history); by the close of 1956 it held fifty percent of India's tread-rubber market, and the multinationals had withdrawn from the business rather than fight for it (the company's milestones). It is the pattern the whole later story repeats: enter underneath the incumbents, win on compound quality, and hold the segment until the economics of fighting stop making sense.

The jump from tread rubber to tyres is the jump from repairing a product to making it - plant, chemistry, capital and brand, all at once. Mappillai made it with a partner: on 5 November 1960 the company was incorporated as a private limited company, manufacturing automobile, aircraft and cycle tyres in technical collaboration with the Mansfield Tire & Rubber Company of Mansfield, Ohio - the early tyres were sold under the trade name "Mansfield Tyres (MRF)" (ET's history). In 1961 MRF went public, and Tamil Nadu's Chief Minister, K. Kamaraj, released the first tyre from the new pilot plant at Tiruvottiyur. The state kept blessing the factory: Industries Minister R. Venkataraman commissioned a new unit in December 1962 (The Hindu's archive), and in June 1963 Prime Minister Nehru laid the foundation stone of its rubber research centre.

Then the company did something no Indian tyre maker had done: it sold to the Americans. In 1964 MRF opened an overseas office in Beirut - one of India's first serious export sorties - and in 1967 it became the first Indian company to export tyres to the United States, the birthplace of tyre technology (NDTV Profit). The Beirut year also gave India an enduring piece of commercial art: the MRF Muscleman, the bare-chested figure holding a tyre aloft, born 1964, which turned an industrial product into a household idea of strength (Mint). By 1970 the company had its second plant. The balloon shed was now a multinational's problem.

Inside the gates, Mappillai ran a patriarchal, prayerful enterprise - major decisions preceded by prayer, absolute loyalty demanded, secrecy absolute, quality uncompromised, with his brothers K.M. Cherian, K.M. Philip and K.M. Mathew as the close circle (Mint's account). Outside the gates, the quality had made MRF worth owning - and twice, someone tried to own it.

The first siege came from a friend. Michelin, the French giant, was MRF's partner in aircraft tyres - the company had climbed from balloons to fighter-aircraft tyres in four decades - and in the early 1990s it moved to take control of its partner. Mappillai, whose distrust of multinationals was by then doctrine, fought the grab and won by rallying India's domestic financial institutions behind the promoter's stake. A second hostile attempt came in 2000, and he saw that one off too (Mint). The control never left the family; it has not since.

The same stubbornness wrote the most famous number in the Indian market. MRF's promoters consistently refused to split the stock, preferring operating performance to market optics (Mint), and the float stayed tiny - a little over three million shares against, for comparison, nearly two billion at TCS (Scroll.in). So the price compounded in plain sight: Rs 1,218 in January 2001; the first Indian share ever to cross Rs 60,000, in March 2017; the first to cross one lakh, in June 2023; and, at Monday's BSE close, Rs 1,25,070.85 for a single share with a face value of ten rupees. The price is not the strategy; it is the receipt.

K.M. Mammen Mappillai died in 2003. The arithmetic of his life's work: from a Rs 10,000 balloon venture to revenues of Rs 2,241 crore in his last year - and, in the financial year just ended, Rs 31,654 crore, with roughly thirty percent of India's tyre market, ahead of Apollo and CEAT at home and Bridgestone and Michelin from abroad (the company's current figures; Mint). Brand Finance ranks MRF the world's second-strongest tyre brand. The family still runs it: sons K.M. Mammen and Arun Mammen, and a fourth generation led by managing director Rahul Mammen Mappillai.

The second identity is cricket's. In 1987 the company founded the MRF Pace Foundation in Chennai - associated with Dennis Lillee and later with a young Glenn McGrath - giving a tyre company the kind of cultural footing the Michelin Guide gives a restaurant guide's parent (Mint's comparison). Generations of Indian fast bowlers came through its gates while the Muscleman held his tyre over the boundary boards.

And on Tuesday, on a day the market was shut, the company this paper can finally tell in full filed its quarter: revenue up 17.4% to Rs 8,660 crore, consolidated net profit down 26.6% to Rs 387 crore on the company's own headline line - the other line of the same package, total comprehensive income attributable to owners, fell 22.8% to Rs 417 crore - as rubber costs jumped 43% year-on-year; and an interim dividend of three rupees a share, declared into the headwind (the filing itself; ETMarkets; Autocar Professional). A down quarter absorbed with the dividend held is not a new scene in this story; it is the same scene, the eighty-first year of it. Somewhere in the file of 1938 there is a liquidated bank and a boy on floorboards; the institution that boy built now weathers commodity cycles the way he taught it to - quietly, with the books closed to optics and the doors open to no one.
